articles.title: CIA Warns of Potential Russian Drone Strikes From Shadow Fleet Vessels
articles.body:
Spain’s El Mundo publication on Wednesday said that Russia may be preparing to launch drone strikes against Southern European countries from shadow fleet vessels passing through the Mediterranean.
Citing a source close to Lithuania’s defense ministry, the report said the warning originated from the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), which has reportedly alerted European governments to the potential threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to El Mundo, such a move would fit into Russia’s broader campaign of “hybrid” operations against NATO members supporting Ukraine. Experts quoted by the outlet said Moscow has so far stopped short of actions that could trigger a direct military response from the alliance. They argue, however, that recent escalations suggest the Kremlin is pushing those boundaries.
This has included increased numbers of drone incursions into Poland, Romania, and the Baltic nations, as well as the attempted use of armed drones at Leipzig Airport and the Wuntsorf airbase, both attributed to Russia.
Russia’s weapon of choice
According to the Lithuanian source cited by El Mundo, any such operation would likely target Spain, France, or Italy using Russia’s Gerbera drones.
“Launched from the sea, hidden in shipping containers; it’s not difficult at all,” the source said.
The report noted that the Gerbera’s compact size gives it an advantage over the larger and more complex Iranian-designed Shahed or Geran attack drones that are widely used by Russia against Ukraine.
Zelensky Says He Would Visit Moscow ‘On a Rocket’
The Gerbera is around 2 meters (6.6 feet) long, has a 2.5-meter (8-feet) wingspan, weighs 18 kilograms (40 pounds), and holds a 5-kilogram (11-pound) warhead.
It has a range between 300 kilometers (186 miles) and 600 kilometers (370 miles), depending on the fuel load and weather conditions, and can travel at speeds of up to 160 kph (100 mph).
A Gerbera-2 drone carrying a 4-kilogram (8.8 pound) fragmentation warhead was recovered off Poland’s coast on Sept. 14. According to the report, the drone was most likely launched from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave rather than from a vessel at sea.
El Mundo also cited British military analyst Keir Giles, who said such attacks could be aimed at disrupting airport operations, starting fires in factories, threatening military installations, or simply a demonstration of Russia’s ability to strike “anywhere in Europe.”
A separate Lithuanian source told the newspaper that Russia wants to show that it can replicate Ukraine’s June 2025 “Spider’s Web” operation, during which small autonomous drones were launched from trucks attacking and damaging 41 Russian strategic military aircraft across multiple air bases deep inside Russia.
Russia’s been practicing the technique
In September 2025, the Ukrainian media outlet Defense Express reported that Russian drones, possibly Gerberas launched from a shadow fleet vessel, had forced the closure of Copenhagen and Oslo airports.
It also said that the Russian manufacturer Zala Aero had practiced launching its reconnaissance and Lancet attack drones from the BK-16E high-speed assault boat in 2020 and again in October 2024.
In February 2026, there were also reports that a Swedish naval unit detected and jammed a drone originating from a Russian signals intelligence vessel near the port city of Malmo where the French aircraft Charles De Gaulle was docked.

articles.title: North Korea tests a guided rocket built like America’s GMLRS
articles.body:
- North Korea test-fired an upgraded, guided 240mm rocket on Sept. 22 that it says can strike targets up to 115 km away, threatening the Seoul area.
- The guided rocket is separate from North Korea's older, unguided 240mm launchers already supplied to Russia for use against Ukraine.
North Korea test-fired an upgraded, precision-guided 240mm rocket on Sept. 22, state media said Sept. 24, claiming the new round can strike targets up to 115 km (71 miles) away, close enough to reach the Seoul metropolitan area from launch positions north of the Demilitarized Zone. North Korea has built the rocket along the same basic concept as the U.S. Army’s GMLRS, the guided rocket fired from HIMARS: take a large-caliber artillery rocket and add a guidance package so it can hit a specific point rather than simply saturating an area.
GMLRS, short for Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System, is the precision rocket the U.S. Army fires from HIMARS, trading the wide dispersal of older unguided rockets for a satellite-guided system that can hit a specific point target dozens of kilometers away. North Korea’s new 240mm rocket follows the same basic concept: take an existing large-caliber artillery rocket and add a guidance package so it can be aimed rather than simply launched en masse.
The Korean Central News Agency said the test was part of North Korea’s five-year defense development plan and involved what it called an “updated 240mm guided rocket.” The agency said the rocket uses an onboard precision guidance system and can reach 100 km (62 miles) on a standard ballistic trajectory, or up to 115 km using a combined glide-and-ballistic flight path, a range and flight profile that puts it in the same general class as extended-range versions of GMLRS.
This guided rocket is a distinct weapon from North Korea’s older 240mm multiple rocket launcher, sometimes called the M1991 by Western analysts, which fires unguided, spin-stabilized rockets in mass salvos with a range of roughly 40 to 60 km. North Korea has supplied that older, unguided system to Russia for use against Ukraine. Ukrainian intelligence and open-source reporting have documented North Korean M1991 launchers, along with M-1989 self-propelled howitzers and ballistic missiles, transferred to Russian forces since late 2024, and Russian troops have used the rockets on the battlefield in Ukraine, according to footage geolocated by Ukrainian military journalists.
North Korea first tested a guided version of the 240mm rocket in May 2024, then tested an upgraded variant again on May 26, 2026, alongside two other systems: an AI-guided tactical cruise missile and a separate, lightweight rocket launcher that Western analysts have compared to HIMARS itself, distinct from the 240mm rocket program. That HIMARS-style launcher first appeared publicly at a 2023 military parade, and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspected it moving toward production during a factory tour Sept. 16 to 18, according to state media.
South Korea’s military has previously tracked North Korean weapons tests independently, though it has not always confirmed Pyongyang’s specific performance claims, and Seoul has not yet issued its own assessment of the Sept. 22 guided rocket test or the range figures North Korea reported.

articles.title: Russia will intensify hybrid attacks against West, NATO, says Danish intelligence
articles.body:
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West in the coming months, Denmark's defense intelligence service said in a new threat assessment on Thursday.
Hybrid warfare and sabotage on European soil gained renewed attention after Germany recently blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, prompting European Union members to call for new sanctions against Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement in hybrid warfare, sabotage operations in NATO countries, or plotting any confrontation.
The Russian embassy to Denmark did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
More frequent attacks expected from Russia
The defense intelligence service said Russia will carry out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO "with greater consequences for the countries targeted than in the past."
It added that there was "a low but growing risk" that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border Russia.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia’s part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it said.
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
He said Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops into a NATO border area, potentially under the pretext of protecting Russian minorities.
"The aim is not to take over the country, but to divide NATO," he said.
A Russian frigate last week fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter sent to photograph it in international waters off Denmark, with one narrowly missing the aircraft, according to the Danish military.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the Danish Resilience Agency said it was likely that Russia would attempt to carry out destructive cyberattacks against Denmark, and it raised its threat level.

articles.title: Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
articles.body:
Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Germany’s Axel Springer media monolith is about to award its highest honor to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, in a ceremony illustrating the incestuous relationship between the mainstream media, the defense tech industry, and the US-Israeli order.
Thiel will receive the ‘2026 Axel Springer Award’ at a ceremony in Berlin on Thursday. According to Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner, Thiel “is one of the rare entrepreneurs who does not merely found or finance companies but helps determine the direction of technological development.”
“He reminds us that progress requires courage and nonconformism,” Dopfner added.
Previous recipients of the Axel Springer Award include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. None of these laureates have proven as controversial as Thiel, however.
According to Status News, employees at Politico and Business Insider – both of which are owned by Axel Springer – have pushed back against the decision. In a letter to management on Tuesday, 120 staffers argued that Thiel, who funded the lawsuit that destroyed Gawker, should not be honored by a company which, in the words of Dopfner, “stands for freedom of speech and a culture of open discussions.”
They’re missing the point. Palantir and Axel Springer are cogs in the same machine. They share an almost identical world view, marked by a devotion to US-Israeli hegemony, a belief that private companies must serve the interests of this hegemony, and a common parent: the CIA.
The CIA connection
During the Cold War, the US saw strategic control of media outlets as key to preventing the rise of socialism and communism in Western Europe. Axel Springer, the anti-communist press baron who gave his name to the company, was a natural ally in this fight. Springer received $7 million in funding from the CIA in 1957, two former agents told The Nation in 1982. Adjusted for inflation, the donation would be equivalent to more than $80 million today.
Although the agents claimed that Springer ended his relationship with the agency in the mid-1970s, declassified documents show that he was still in contact with the United States Information Agency (USIA) – which funded pro-American news outlets – in the early 1980s. In 1982, Springer was introduced to CIA Director William Casey as “a strong supporter of the United States” who “is doing all he can to strengthen the ties between the United States and Europe.”
Thiel, who co-founded PayPal, launched Palantir in 2003 with the stated goal of taking “the approaches that PayPal had used to fight fraud…into other contexts, like fighting terrorism.” The CIA took notice, and invested $2 million in the company in 2005 via its in-house venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel.
“I wish I had Palantir when I was director,” former CIA chief George Tenet – who set up In-Q-Tel – told Forbes magazine in 2013. “I wish we had the tool of its power.”
The Axel Springer investment pays off
In both cases, the CIA’s investments paid off. Axel Springer is now Europe’s largest publisher, and owns Politico, Business Insider, Bild, Die Welt, The Telegraph, and nearly a dozen other outlets. The American deep state continues to finance its operations, with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the State Department’s National Endowment for Democracy (NED) pumping just under $34 million into Politico between 2016 and 2025.
In return, Axel Springer has openly pledged fealty to American neoliberalism. Whereas Springer himself described his first newspaper, the Hamburger Abendblatt, as “geared to the underdog and the little man,” staff at Axel Springer publications are today required to adhere to the following code of conduct:
- “We stand up for freedom, free speech, the rule of law, and democracy”
- “We support the right of existence of the State of Israel and oppose all forms of anti-Semitism”
- “We advocate the alliance between the United States of America and Europe”
- “We uphold the principles of a free market economy”
- “We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of discrimination”
In practice, this means that Axel Springer publications will feature lively debate over ‘red versus blue’ politics in the US and Europe, but will never question key tenets of US foreign policy, including America’s alliance with Israel, its dominance over Europe through NATO, and the legitimacy of its proxy war with Russia in Ukraine.
The world according to Palantir
More than two decades after taking CIA money, Palantir is now the largest of the Silicon Valley defense kingpins, and a synonym for the burgeoning surveillance- and military-tech sector as a whole. Palantir is valued at around $427 billion, a figure bolstered by lucrative contracts with the US’ defense and intelligence agencies, including all six branches of the US military, the CIA, FBI, NSA, and DIA.
Palantir’s flagship product is an operating system called ‘Gotham’, which is essentially a data analytics platform for military, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Gotham pulls together and analyses existing data that may otherwise take days to sift through. For example, if US Central Command is planning a missile strike in a foreign country, Gotham can combine maps and satellite footage from that country, data from other agencies, including human intelligence from the CIA and signals intelligence from the NSA, and local surveillance data to present CENTCOM with potential targets for military strikes.
Palantir’s international customers include the British, Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, NATO, domestic intelligence agencies in France and Germany, and police departments in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, among others.
However, Palantir is not a mercenary company selling its products to anyone with money. According to CEO Alex Karp, Palantir is inseparable from the US deep state, and “was founded to strengthen US national security, to protect Americans and their freedom.”
Because we get asked a lot.
The Technological Republic, in brief.
1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation.
2. We must rebel…
Earlier this year, Karp set out Palantir’s world view in a manifesto, which RT already covered in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series. In the 22-point bulletin, Karp argued that “the engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation,” that “free and democratic societies” must pursue AI superweapons to preserve the hegemony of the US, which “has advanced progressive values” more than “any other nation on the planet.”
In separate comments, Karp has described pro-Palestinian protesters as a “cancerous” influence on American politics, while Palantir describes its work with the Israeli state as “in line with our global support of US allies and liberal democracies.”
Critics called Karp’s manifesto “technofascist,” but it differs little in substance from Axel Springer’s code of conduct. Karp’s remaining points wade into US-centric culture war territory, but the core argument of both documents is the same: the US and Israel are a benevolent force and the private sector has a duty to aid their foreign policy goals; by argument, in the case of Axel Springer, and by force, in the case of Palantir.
The incestuous security state
Back in Berlin, the guest speakers at Thursday’s ceremony further illustrate the incestuous relationship between Axel Springer, Palantir, and the US-Israeli order. Before Dopfner hands him his award, Thiel will be lauded by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a self-described “Zionist fanatic” who was appointed head of the network following its acquisition last year by billionaire and pro-Israel megadonor David Ellison, whose family has donated more than $26 million to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since 2014.
Before the acquisition, Weiss repeatedly complained about CBS’ supposedly “anti-Israel bias.” Once in control of the network, she set about hiring pro-Israel editors and reportedly intervening personally in stories concerning the Jewish state.
Thursday’s ceremony will also feature a questions-and-answers session with PayPal co-founder Max Levchin, a vocal defender of the NSA amid Edward Snowden’s revelations of warrantless wiretapping.
The award is equivalent to an ‘Employee of the Month’ prize from one department of the same company to another. It’s like USAID and CIA agents meeting for after-work drinks, or Weiss congratulating the IDF for its service.
Dopfner, Thiel, Weiss and Levchin understand they’re all on the same team. Anyone who’s followed RT’s ‘Wired for War’ series will grasp this. The only people yet to figure it out, apparently, are the Politico and Business Insider staffers complaining about the threat posed by Thiel to “Axel Springer’s own commitment to freedom.”
Thursday’s ceremony might help them understand the true nature of the power they serve a little clearer.

articles.title: Russia slams Kyiv with ballistic missiles as Ukrainians brace for harsh winter
articles.body:
Russia slams Kyiv with ballistic missiles as Ukrainians brace for harsh winter
Russia on Thursday hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones, killing two people, while a strike on a farm in the Kharkiv region killed six, according to Ukrainian officials. As autumn approaches, Ukrainians are bracing for a tough winter following Moscow's intensifying attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.

Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least two people in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, with the Ukrainian capital rocked by multiple powerful explosions after authorities issued a missile alert.
More than 20 blasts were heard on Thursday, according to AFP journalists, after the Ukrainian Air Force warned that Russian ballistic missiles were headed for the city.
"Once again, the main targets of (the Russian) attack were Kyiv and civilian infrastructure – residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy facilities and logistics. Two people are already known to have been killed," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
In a message on X, Zelensky noted that "Russia will not end this war without pressure. As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky. Once again, the main targets of their strike were Kyiv and civilian infrastructure, residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy infrastructure, and logistics."
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"Explosions in Kyiv. The capital is under ballistic missile attack. Remain in shelters!" Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko wrote in a Telegram message.
The strikes came as Zelensky was meeting members of the US Congress as part of his trip to the United States to request stronger sanctions against Moscow.
In Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, a Russian strike on a farm killed six people, said Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky.
The regional prosecutor's office said the farm in the Chuguiv district, southeast of Kharkiv, was hit as employees were sorting vegetables at a storage facility.
It published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse, where what appear to be piles of apples were scattered across the floor, with a gaping hole in the roof.
Read moreZelensky accuses Putin of using nationals of 47 countries to fight Ukraine war
Kyiv residents brace for harsh winter
The barrage was the latest in an intensifying exchange of long-range attacks, with both Kyiv and Moscow signalling at the UN that they will escalate strikes and dimming prospects for diplomacy.
The first days of autumn chill have only barely set in over Kyiv, but winter is already dominating conversations among residents, who are making plans in case Russian strikes once again knock out the energy system.
The shadow of last winter hangs over Kyiv, which was plunged into darkness and bitter cold for weeks when Russian forces struck the country's power and heating infrastructure while temperatures dropped as low as -20C.
As Russia stepped up assaults on Kyiv, the question of what to do this winter is particularly pressing for families with children, said Oleksandra Matveieva, founder of a Facebook group for mothers.
"Now it seems Russians have started bombing Kyiv heavily," she said.
"Immediately, people, mostly mothers, started writing: 'we're ready to leave anywhere, as long as it's not too far and expensive'."
Travel Mama Club, originally founded for travelling mothers before evolving into an advice forum during the war, has recently seen a surge in publications concerning accommodation in relatively safer western Ukraine, or abroad.
"People are looking for a Plan B, even booking refundable apartments," she said. "They still don't know yet whether they will actually leave."
Russia has over the past month stepped up its attacks on the capital and air raid alerts urging locals to seek shelter due to incoming drones and missiles are now a nightly and, increasingly, daily occurrence.
If it used to target Kyiv mainly during the hours of darkness, Moscow now attacks more in broad daylight. The alerts paralyse life across the city – especially in schools and hospitals, which follow strict safety protocols.
'Critically cold'
The strikes are part of escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine, which UN investigators warn are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches.
US President Donald Trump said last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities, but the proposal failed to materialise.
Zelensky told the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday that, "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too."
Ukrainian authorities have rushed to reinforce the battered energy system. The energy ministry said the country has already repaired 4.8 gigawatts of generating capacity and plans to restore or build over 10 gigawatts this year.
The International Energy Agency said in September last year that Ukraine had about 38 gigawatts of despatchable power generation capacity before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last winter, demand peaked at 18GW, while the capacity had dropped to 11GW after years of attacks, the agency said.
Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who has been criticised by the government for failing to present a clear strategy, has said the city completed 80 percent of its preparations ahead of winter.
The CEO of Ukraine's main gas provider Naftogaz, Sergiy Fedorenko, acknowledged Russia's strikes were "stronger, broader, more dangerous".
"But we prepared for this the whole time between heating seasons and we will withstand these blows over this difficult winter," he told AFP.
Besides heating and energy, there are fears Russia may seek to destroy water supplies, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmygal said in August.
Residents are making their own preparations, dusting off the generators, portable batteries and hot water bottles they relied on last year, while making adjustments.
Some hold on to the hope the weather will be milder this year.
"If it's cold again, as critically cold as it was last year, I will leave," said Matveieva, who has a daughter.
"I'll take her and get her out of here."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Zelensky to UNGA: Putin’s war in Ukraine will spread more evil without international pressure
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia “will not end this war without pressure” in his address to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday.
He noted that, while he believes that this upcoming winter could be difficult for Ukrainians, his army will make Russia’s winters difficult as well.
"Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," he said.
"No Russian official ever imagined that 'Army General Winter,' which had fought on Russia's side for centuries, would one day switch sides and support those defending themselves from Russia. We will make that happen this winter if Russia continues to target our energy system and our heating," Zelensky said.
He also called for robust diplomatic efforts to help de-escalate the war before winter sets in.
Zelensky: Putin is 'patient zero' that needs to be stopped before he leaves behind more evil
Zelensky then called Russian President Vladimir Putin “patient zero” and added that "the longer Putin is able to wage war, the more evil he will leave behind in this world.”
He also stressed that more sanctions against the Kremlin were needed, along with continued support for Ukraine.
"Yes, sometimes it may seem that Ukraine is focused only on war because we speak about weapons, we speak about defense, and sanctions against the aggressor. But Ukrainians did not choose this war. We choose not to die, not to lose our country, our families, not to lose our independence, our freedom," he said.
Shortly before Zelensky addressed the assembly, Russia launched an attack on Kyiv, killing at least two people.
The attack lasted from morning into the evening in one of the heaviest strikes since Russia began hitting Kyiv and nearby areas with faster and high-flying jet drones that are harder to intercept.
“Every such attack happens because the pressure on the aggressor has never become total, and Russia believes it can continue to bet on ballistic terror,” Zelensky said.
“Right now, the United States has an opportunity to respond strongly. We need ballistic interceptors to protect lives.”
Zelensky says Ukraine released two North Korean soldiers to South Korea
Zelensky also revealed that Ukrainian troops recently captured two North Korean soldiers, but sent them to South Korea. 
“One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. He was shocked that fate didn’t let him die. This is how they raise people in the north,” he said.
South Korea did not confirm any details about the North Korean soldiers out of concern for their families still inside the DPRK.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ethiopia appears to receive Chinese FK-2000 air defense systems
articles.body:
- Social media footage reportedly shows at least two Chinese-made FK-2000 air defense units heading toward Ethiopia's Amhara region, likely supplied via the UAE.
- An open-source analyst said the systems will likely protect Bahir Dar Airport, where ENDF aircraft and drones and UAE-operated Akıncı drones are reportedly based.
Ethiopia’s military appears to have gained a new shield for its drone fleet: Chinese-made FK-2000 air defense systems, most likely delivered through the United Arab Emirates.
Video shared on TikTok reportedly shows at least two of the truck-mounted systems on the road to Amhara, the northern region where government troops have been fighting Fano militias for more than three years. No government has confirmed the delivery. It is not known how many systems Ethiopia received, when they arrived, or who paid for them.
“The Chinese-made FK-2000 short-range air defence systems will likely be deployed around Bahir Dar Airport in northern Ethiopia, protecting ENDF aircraft and drones stationed there alongside UAE-operated Akıncı drones,” said open-source analyst Rich Tedd.
Bahir Dar, the regional capital, has served as a drone base before. Satellite images from October 2022 appeared to show Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 drones parked at its airport. The Akıncı is a larger combat drone from the same Turkish manufacturer, Baykar.
The FK-2000 works much like Russia’s Pantsir. A single eight-wheeled truck carries both missiles and guns. Its 12 radar-guided missiles can reach targets about 25 km (15.5 miles) away and up to 12 km (39,000 feet) high, while twin 30 mm cannons deal with threats that get closer. The system is built to bring down drones, helicopters, aircraft and cruise missiles, day or night and in bad weather. It is made by China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation.
The same weapon has turned up elsewhere in Africa, and the trail has led back to the UAE before. Chad was earlier reported to have received two FK-2000 units. In August 2025, The Defence Blog reported claims that systems the UAE had bought from China were sent to Chad and then moved into Sudan, to the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group. Abu Dhabi did not confirm that transfer.
In Ethiopia, the systems are heading into a hot war zone. The army has fought Fano, an Amhara nationalist militia movement, since April 2023, and has leaned heavily on drone strikes. Local media and rights groups have reported repeated civilian deaths from those strikes.
Fano launched offensives across Amhara in March 2026, disrupting preparations for the June 1 national elections in parts of the region. The army sent reinforcements and struck back, but conflict data from ACLED showed May on track to be Fano’s busiest month of the year. In late April, Fano fighters reportedly staged a surprise attack near Bahir Dar itself.
Fano is not known to fly combat aircraft, so it is unclear exactly what threat the FK-2000s are meant to stop.

articles.title: Russian Radars and Drone Launch Site Damaged by Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian radar stations, an attack drone launch facility, and a fuel depot across occupied parts of the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, Ukraine’s military said.
According to a statement published by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), the strikes were carried out on Wednesday, Sept. 23, and overnight into Thursday, Sept. 24.

Near occupied Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit a facility allegedly used by Russian units to store, prepare, and launch attack drones.
“Striking such facilities is one of the priority areas of combat operations by Ukraine’s Defense Forces,” the General Staff said.
The military did not disclose the weapons used, the number of drones potentially stored at the site, or the extent of the damage.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify the reported results.
Russian air surveillance radars hit
Ukraine also reported striking two Russian radar stations in the occupied part of the Zaporizhzhia region.
A Russian 35N6 Kasta radar was hit near Chekhohrad, formerly known as Novohrodivka, while a P-18 radar was targeted near Akymivka, according to the General Staff.
The 35N6 Kasta is a Russian mobile surveillance radar designed to detect aircraft and other aerial targets, including objects flying at extremely low altitudes. It can transmit targeting information to air defense command posts.
The Soviet-designed P-18 is a mobile early-warning radar operating in the meter-wave band. It detects aerial targets, determines their distance and direction, and passes the information to air defense units.

By targeting radar stations, Ukraine seeks to weaken Russia’s ability to detect incoming aircraft, missiles and drones, and to coordinate its air defense systems.
Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian surveillance and air defense equipment. In August, Ukrainian forces struck another Kasta radar, a drone training center, repair facilities, and military depots across occupied territories.
Earlier in September, Ukrainian forces also reportedly hit a P-18 radar, drone production facilities, and a Pantsir-S2 air defense system in Russia’s Taganrog.
Fuel depot targeted
The General Staff also reported a strike on a Russian fuel and lubricants depot near Velyka Bilozerka, also in the occupied part of the Zaporizhzhia region.
Such depots supply fuel to Russian vehicles, generators, and other military equipment operating near the front.
The latest operation followed another series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian drone infrastructure. On Sept. 17 and overnight into Sept. 18, Ukrainian forces hit an Orion drone control station at the Saki airfield in occupied Crimea, another attack drone launch site near Donetsk, and two military depots in the Luhansk region.
“Work against key military targets of the Russian aggressor continues,” the General Staff added.

Russian Drone and Missile Barrage Damages Kyiv Maternity Hospital and Odesa Medical Facility
Russian forces launched a massive missile and drone strike across Ukraine on September 24, killing at least two people in Kyiv and damaging medical facilities in the capital and Odesa, despite Ukrainian air defenses intercepting over 200 drones and seven advanced missiles.
Russian forces launched a large-scale overnight assault on Ukraine, deploying a mix of anti-ship and ballistic missiles alongside a swarm of 282 strike drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on September 24.
Ukrainian air defense systems successfully intercepted a significant portion of the complex barrage, neutralizing four Zircon cruise missiles, three ballistic missiles, one S8000 “Banderol” jet-powered loitering munition, and 219 unmanned aerial vehicles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Despite the high interception rate, the Air Force reported direct enemy hits in 13 locations and falling debris in 10 others, noting that the primary attack directions were the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
In southern Odesa, the strikes injured two people, according to Oleh Kiper, head of the Odesa Regional State Administration. Kiper stated that the attack damaged the roof and top floor of a local medical facility, while blast waves shattered windows across ten residential buildings and a school.
The Ukrainian capital also sustained widespread damage. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU) reported that the aftermath of the attack was recorded across four distinct districts of Kyiv, with two civilians reported dead and at least eight more injured.
The agency confirmed damage to multiple residential buildings, an administrative center, a maternity hospital, and a clinical diagnostic center. The assault also impacted the city’s critical energy and logistics infrastructure, damaging a post office, warehouses, nine private homes, and dozens of civilian vehicles.
A Russian strike on Kyiv’s data centers and communications infrastructure had recently left around 100,000 households in the capital and surrounding region without internet connectivity. The attack damaged facilities belonging to internet service providers Pavutyna and UTELS, while a strike on a traffic exchange point extended disruptions to users in Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated that Moscow is intentionally targeting data infrastructure to disable early warning systems, aiming to cut civilians off from life-saving air raid notifications.

articles.title: US Needs Ukrainian Expertise to Integrate Drones With Air Defense Radars
articles.body:
- Category
- World
US Needs Ukrainian Expertise to Integrate Drones With Air Defense Radars
Ukraine is ready to sign a landmark drone-defense deal with the United States, CBS News reported on September 23, citing three sources familiar with the matter.
According to the outlet, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is prepared to sign the agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City this week.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deal has not yet been signed, however. The outlet's sources indicated it could instead be finalized at a later date, with the timing dependent on when the US is ready to sign.
Over the past year, the US Department of Defense and its Ukrainian counterpart have developed a framework to expand testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US, CBS News reported.
Sources with direct knowledge of the deal described it as going beyond contracts for a handful of Ukrainian companies. It would instead let leading Ukrainian defense firms work directly with American counterparts and the US military.
Deborah Fairlamb, founding partner of Green Flag Ventures, an American venture capital firm investing in Ukrainian defense technology, emphasized that the deal's value will hinge on transferring Ukraine's operational know-how alongside its hardware.
"It's not just about having the tech. It's about how the tech is used," she told CBS News.
The war with Iran has underscored the value of Ukraine's defense industry to the US and its allies, CBS News noted.
In its first days, Iran began targeting American military installations across the Middle East with Shahed one-way attack drones, the same type Russia has used against Ukrainian cities. Because the US and Gulf states initially lacked cost-effective means of interception, Kyiv sent drone interceptors and pilots to help.
Ukraine has since signed defense agreements with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, among other countries, matching foreign financing with its growing defense industry.
Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine aims to produce 10 million drones this year. By comparison, the US Army acquired roughly 50,000 in 2025, according to former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.
CBS News also detailed previously unreported episodes from the war's opening days.
In March, then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll asked Eric Schmidt, the former Google CEO who founded the US drone company Perennial Autonomy, to supply 13,000 Merops interceptor drones and 10,000 Bumblebee reconnaissance and strike drones to the Middle East.
The drones reached the US military within days but took weeks to become operational because Ukrainian components arrived late, according to multiple sources familiar with the shipments.
According to CBS News, Merops drones use AI beacons manufactured by Ukraine’s Sine Engineering as well as Ukrainian warheads.
Washington's efforts to absorb the lessons of Ukraine's drone warfare have been uneven, the outlet added.
CBS News reported that Ukrainian expertise was also required to integrate the Merops drones into US air-defense radars before they could be used in combat.
In August, the US Army phased out a drone battalion tasked with studying those lessons, while the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program invited American and select foreign companies, primarily Ukrainian ones, to compete for contracts.
The program aims to buy more than 200,000 drones by 2027, and Ukrainian manufacturer Skyfall won its first round earlier this year.
CBS News stated that it had reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment on the status of the drone deal and on the use of Ukrainian technology to defend bases in the Middle East.
The prospective agreement builds on a run of steps that have already brought Ukrainian systems into the American military ecosystem.
On July 22, Ukraine and the US signed a bilateral statement of intent establishing a framework for the temporary export of Ukrainian unmanned systems to the US for testing by the Pentagon.
By July 31, F-Drones had delivered the first 2,000 F10 FPV drones under the $1 billion Drone Dominance Program, making the F10 the first Ukrainian drone authorized for export to the US under the initiative.
Ukrainian personnel have also trained US service members at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia on the Sky Map software, a command-and-control platform used to identify Shahed-type threats and coordinate interceptor drones.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles rock Kyiv as air defenses engaged
articles.body:
Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv kills 2, injures 8 after day of drone strikes
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Two people were killed and 8 others were injured as Russian ballistic missile explosions rocked Kyiv overnight on Sept. 24.
At the same time missiles were battering the capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky was meeting with members of the U.S. Congress, discussing the recently passed Lindsey Graham law while attending the U.N. General Assembly. 
"Right now, the United States has an opportunity to respond strongly," Zelensky wrote on X. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives. Sanctions against Russia and those helping it make money must be implemented."
Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent he believed the timing of the attack was deliberate.
"Russia is clearly trying to influence the positions of the U.S. and Ukraine and push us to accept its terms, which would effectively amount to capitulation. It is also trying to pressure the U.S. ahead of the elections so that Washington puts even more pressure on us," Yurchyshyn said.
He argued that the appropriate response would be for the U.S. and its partners to provide greater support to Ukraine and tighten sanctions against Russia.
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, according to the Air Force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
"We had three waves of ballistic attacks. Today in Kyiv, 60% of the ballistic missiles were shot down," Zelensky told reporters at a press conference in New York on Sept. 24. "It is important. We would like more to be shot down, but today it was 60%, not 10% and not zero."
Zelensky added that there had been attacks earlier this year in which Ukraine intercepted none of the incoming ballistic missiles, attributing this to shortages of interceptor missiles.
Loud explosions were first heard in the city center of Ukraine's capital at around 1:00 a.m. local time, Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko said.
Ukraine's Air Force also warned that a ballistic missile was headed toward Kyiv after an air raid alert had been declared in Kyiv at 12:59 a.m.
"I got woken up by the sound of an explosion, slept through the air raid alert. When I checked my phone, I saw alerts for incoming missiles and went to my hallway as a series of explosions blasted out, one of them set off car alarms near my flat," War Editor Chris York said.
Then another ballistic missile was headed toward Ukraine's capital at 1:27 a.m., the Air Force said.
"It was quiet for about 30 minutes until another wave of ballistic missiles came in, I counted eight explosions," York said.
A third wave of ballistic missile explosions rocked the city again at around 1:52 a.m. local time, he added.
Updates from authorities
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that paramedics were headed to sites in the city's Solomyanskyi, Svyatoshynskyi, and Podilskyi districts as Russian missiles continued to target the city.
In the Dniprovskyi district, debris fell into a residential building courtyard, where there could be people trapped under rubble, he said. Debris also fell onto an administrative building in the district.
"In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on a parking lot near a medical facility. Several cars caught fire. Emergency services are en route," Klitschko said.
Kyiv City Maternity Hospital No. 2 was partially damaged in the attack, with windows and doors on the first through fifth floors damaged, as well as windows in the laundry and boiler room, Kyiv's Health Department said. No patients or medical staff were injured, as they were sheltering during the attack.
At 2:05 a.m., during the height of the attack, a baby boy was born in the hospital's shelter, where medical staff continued providing care.
"Even on such a terrible night, life goes on," Tetiana Mostepan, head of Kyiv's Health Department, said. "Our medical staff remain with patients under any circumstances and do everything possible to ensure that care is provided on time."
Although there were no casualties in the maternity hospital, one person was killed in a nearby parking lot, Klitschko said, adding that a medical diagnostic center was also damaged.
The attack also destroyed the production facility of Ukrainian jewellery business Dukachi, the company told the Kyiv Independent.
"When we arrived, we saw two groups of firefighters and realized that our premises were burning," co-founders Ana and Liza Knyzhenko said. "When we ran up, we saw a wall of fire. We understood that this was the end, that it was hell, and that nothing had survived."
The company said the building was effectively destroyed, with only some walls and partitions remaining. Equipment, furniture, and stock inside were burned, leaving the facility unusable and forcing the business to rebuild its production from scratch.
Dukachi said the loss was particularly difficult for a small business that had spent eight years building up the production facility. "We don't have programs or resources that would allow us to recover quickly. Everything will have to be rebuilt at our own expense, and that is very expensive and will take a long time," the co-founders said.
Russia regularly strikes civilian infrastructure and cities across Ukraine in fatal missile and drone attacks.
The prior day, on Sept. 23, a series of deadly Russian drone strikes on Kyiv killed two people and injured at least 43 others during the morning.
Railway infrastructure, residential buildings, and a historic market were damaged in the Russian attack.
On Sept. 22, Russian jet-powered drones struck Kyiv, injuring at least eight people and hitting sites across several districts of the capital, authorities said.

He strongly criticised Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, questioning why North Korean soldiers were giving their lives in a war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian and South Korean estimates indicate North Korea has deployed approximately 15,000 soldiers to support Russia’s war effort since 2024, primarily in the Kursk border region.
Zelenskyy provided no further details regarding the transfer.
Ukrainian forces captured the two North Korean soldiers in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025, in the first known apprehension of Pyongyang’s troops since their deployment to the conflict in 2024. Zelenskyy had previously stated he would consider returning the soldiers to North Korean leader Kim in exchange for Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not deny Zelenskyy’s remarks, but it also declined to confirm operational details of the transfer, citing individual safety and family protection.
The issue was a key topic during a July summit in Ankara, Turkiye, where President Lee Jae Myung met Zelenskyy.
Senior presidential spokesperson Kang Yoo-jung stated afterwards that both leaders agreed to resolve the status of North Korean POWs in Ukraine in accordance with international law and humanitarian principles, while respecting the free will of those involved. This built on a prior agreement reached during the South Korea-Ukraine foreign ministers’ meeting in March, where both nations pledged to cooperate on the POW issue under the same humanitarian framework.

articles.title: What we know about CIA warning of Russian drone threat to southern Europe
articles.body:
The US has warned southern states of a possible Moscow attack that would see Russia fire 600 km-range drones from commercial ships at Spain, France and Italy. We examine what is known and how the threat is mounting.
US intelligence services have shared a report with several European countries pointing to a possible Russian operation using drones against targets in Spain, France or Italy, according to Spanish media.
The information was first revealed by journalist Xavier Colás — a former Russia correspondent — in the Spanish newspaper El Mundo. It traces the origin of the alert to CIA director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow last August, and sets out a very specific attack scenario: drones launched from merchant vessels disguised as ordinary commercial traffic.
The Gerbera, a cheap and hard-to-detect weapon
According to information gathered by anonymous sources in Lithuania's Ministry of Defence, and reported by El Mundo, the device in question would be the Gerbera, a small Russian drone (barely two metres long and weighing 18 kilos) capable of travelling up to 600 kilometres at around 160 km/h.
Its limited explosive payload — between four and five kilos — is not intended to cause mass destruction, but to have a symbolic and disruptive effect: temporarily shutting down an airport, starting a fire, or demonstrating that Moscow can strike at Europe's rear without having to cross any land border.
This method is not just a distant hypothesis. The Kremlin has already tested launching drones from maritime platforms. Only last February, a Swedish naval unit detected a drone taking off from a Russian intelligence vessel in the Öresund Strait. Add to this the precedent set by the armed-drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany, which Berlin attributes to Russian intelligence, and the episode of 19 unarmed drones flying over Polish airspace a year ago.
Why southern Europe, and not only the eastern flank
The Kremlin's logic, according to analysts consulted by the Spanish newspaper, is driven not by geographical proximity but by political vulnerability. British expert Keir Giles, a specialist in Russian military strategy, argues that Moscow will look for "the weakest point in Europe", explicitly naming countries such as Spain, which lack integrated air defence systems suited to this type of threat.
This idea ties directly into a warning issued months ago by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte: a Russian missile would take barely ten minutes longer to reach Madrid than to reach Warsaw. Rutte sought to dismantle the perception that southern Europe lies outside the "eastern flank" and is therefore beyond the radius of risk posed by the war that Russia launched against Ukraine in 2022, which threatens the entire continent.
Intimidation using drones launched from the Mediterranean, slower but just as symbolic, fits that same message: distance is no longer a guarantee of security for any European country.
Spain, France and Italy also share another risk factor highlighted in the investigation: all three will hold elections in 2027 and have political forces capable of capitalising on the social fatigue generated by years of war in Ukraine (despite Trump's stated desire to end the conflict before winter) — something that Vladimir Putin's government could try to exploit with a low-cost action and high media impact.
Sánchez, defence spending and tension with Washington
The report comes at a particularly delicate moment for Spain in security terms. Pedro Sánchez's government has been reluctant to raise defence spending to the new threshold demanded by NATO, a stance that has led to open tension with Donald Trump and to an almost broken bilateral relationship. One of the latest examples was seen at the UN General Assembly, where Sánchez refused to attend the reception hosted by Trump in New York.
In this context, an intelligence alert of this kind adds further pressure on Moncloa: the lack of investment in air-defence and anti-missile systems is a weak point laid bare just as the perception of a direct threat to Spanish soil grows.
The Russian diaspora and asset ties on the Costa del Sol
The debate about Spain's exposure to Russian interests is not limited to the military sphere. For years, various journalistic investigations have documented the presence of assets linked to circles around the Kremlin along the Andalusian coast. Among the best-known cases is that of Liudmila Ocheretnaya — formerly Liudmila Putina — Vladimir Putin's ex-wife, who together with her current husband, Artur Ocheretny, came to own two luxury homes in the Lomas del Rey complex (Marbella) worth 2.2 million euros.
Those reports at the time already pointed to an urgent sale of those properties for fear of being included on the European Union sanctions list, after the United Kingdom had already sanctioned her.
Subsequent journalistic investigations have continued to document the web of companies and foundations linked to Ocheretny and his circle, keeping alive the question of the real extent of Russian economic interests, direct or indirect, on Spanish territory. There has been no recent public confirmation that the properties were in fact sold, nor of Ocheretnaya's current residence status on the Costa del Sol.
A threat Europe can no longer treat as distant
The report cited by El Mundo itself recalls that Moscow has for months been operating "below the threshold of war", combining isolated acts of sabotage with tests of reaction such as those carried out in Poland or Germany.
What is new now is that, according to the CIA, this pattern of escalation could spread to the Mediterranean, shattering the false sense of distance that for years has protected countries such as Spain, at least in the collective imagination. As Rutte sums it up, in today's Europe a difference of ten minutes no longer separates a safe country from one at risk.

articles.title: CIA reportedly warns of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy with sea-launched drones
articles.body:
CIA reportedly warns of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy with sea-launched drones
Spanish newspaper El Mundo has learned from its sources that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has warned of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy using drones launched from ships at sea.
Source: European Pravda, citing an El Mundo report
Details: The newspaper reports that European foreign ministries have received a detailed report prepared following CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
According to information from the Lithuanian government, Russia plans to launch Gerbera drones with a range of 600 km from ships. Russia is thus reportedly preparing new drone attacks in Europe, this time targeting Mediterranean countries.
"They will use drones launched from the sea, concealed in a container on a ship. It is not difficult at all," a source told the newspaper.
El Mundo's sources say the governments of Spain, France and Italy have also been informed that Russia was preparing a possible drone operation against one of these countries. The warning coincides with an unusual move by Emmanuel Macron: after convening a meeting of the Defence Council on 16 September, two days later he invited the leaders of all parties and candidates in the 2027 presidential election to the Élysée Palace.
Several defence analysts interviewed by the newspaper confirmed that they were aware of the existence of a CIA report that had been circulated among European foreign ministries.
The attacks are reportedly being prepared specifically against France, Italy and Spain because elections will be held there in 2027 and right-wing political forces are already gaining support.
El Mundo says the main purpose of the Russian operation would not be to cause significant destruction. With an explosive payload of around four to five kilograms, a Gerbera drone would more likely be used to shut down an airport, start a fire, fly over a military facility or demonstrate that Russia is capable of reaching Europe's rear areas.
Background:
- Moscow has repeatedly stated that supplying Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and military advisers makes Western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets.
- However, Russia has so far sought to avoid crossing the "threshold of war" by refraining from actions that could provoke a coordinated NATO response, while testing the Alliance's reaction through individual incidents in Poland and the Baltic states. In particular, on 15 September, Italian fighter jets on a NATO patrol mission shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace. On 23 September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace.

Ukraine Has Chance to End War With Russia Before Winter, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine has a chance to end Russia’s war before winter, but reaching that goal will depend on US political will, increased pressure on Moscow, and additional American military technology, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Wall Street Journal on September 23, Zelenskyy outlined the conditions he believes could create an opportunity to reach what he described as a just peace within the next two months.
“We have a chance to stop and end this war before winter, if… There are several ‘ifs.’ Of course, the first ‘if’ is always will. The will of the United States, especially the president. It is precisely about the political will to end this war,” Zelenskyy said in the interview.
At the same time, the Ukrainian president said political will alone would not be sufficient to change Russia’s position and called for additional pressure on Vladimir Putin.
The second condition, Zelenskyy said, is access to US technology and additional weapons, particularly air defense interceptors needed to protect Ukraine during the coming winter.
“The second ‘if’ is technology. We need some technologies from the United States. We have our experience, we are always ready to share it, but we need something from the US. We need a ‘winter package’: missiles for Patriot systems. Only the US produces them now,” Zelenskyy said.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Zelenskyy raised the proposed “winter package” during his meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York on September 22, requesting additional weapons and Patriot air defense capabilities. Zelenskyy also said he expects Washington to pursue an agreement aimed at stopping attacks on energy infrastructure.
Kyiv has made additional Patriot interceptors one of its main defense priorities ahead of winter. Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine had calculated a requirement of around 300 Patriot missiles for the winter period—approximately 100 per month.
Ukraine has also been discussing licenses that would eventually allow Patriot interceptors to be produced domestically. Zelenskyy has said, however, that securing missiles for immediate use remains a higher priority because establishing new production capacity would take time.
Zelenskyy had previously said Ukraine was prepared to take reciprocal de-escalation steps if Russia stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and food exports.

articles.title: US Democrat senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US Democratic senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
US Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen urged President Donald Trump on Wednesday to press Chinese President Xi Jinping over Beijing's support for Iran, accusing Chinese companies of providing Tehran with economic and military assistance.
The senior Democrat said Trump should use an upcoming summit with Xi to demand action against Chinese firms accused of supplying Iran with satellite imagery and components used in its missile and drone programmes, as well as helping Tehran circumvent sanctions on its oil exports.
Speaking in the Senate, Shaheen cited reports that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese entities before carrying out a missile attack that killed three American soldiers and wounded four others.
She also pointed to China's role as the leading buyer of Iranian oil, saying around 90% of Iran's oil exports go to the country, providing Tehran with billions of dollars in revenue and a "critical economic lifeline".
Chinese and Hong Kong-based companies have also supplied components used in Iranian ballistic missiles and drones, Shaheen said.
"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," she told the Senate.
Shaheen called on Trump to "use his leverage" with Xi to stop Chinese companies from providing satellite imagery, missile and drone components and access to markets for sanctioned Iranian oil.
She also urged the Trump administration to step up enforcement of existing sanctions against Chinese entities accused of helping Iran.
"And if China doesn't stop, Congress should impose additional consequences," she said.
Shaheen linked China's relationship with Iran to its continued purchases of Russian energy, arguing that Beijing was helping finance conflicts involving both Tehran and Moscow, despite the US, alongside Israel, starting the war on Iran.
She said Trump should consider using powers contained in recently enacted legislation targeting Russia to impose penalties on Chinese buyers of Russian energy.
China was "the top funder of the war in Ukraine, as well as being one of the top funders of the war in Iran", Shaheen said.
Shaheen's call for tougher pressure on China comes despite broad public opposition to the US war with Iran, particularly among Democrats.
A Pew Research Center poll conducted in March found 59% of Americans believed the US had made the wrong decision in using military force against Iran, while 61% disapproved of Trump's handling of the conflict.
Opposition was especially strong among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 88% of whom said the decision to use force was wrong and 90% of whom disapproved of Trump's handling of the war.
More recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has also found support for Trump's handling of the conflict remains weak, with only 34% approving of his strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Nuclear arms unlikely to be deployed in Lithuania soon despite parliament consent — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Nuclear weapons will not appear on Lithuanian territory in the near future, despite the decision by the Seimas (parliament) to lift the ban on their deployment, Ruslan Pankratov, a member of the Officers of Russia expert council, deputy chairman of the Union of Political Emigrants of Europe, and a former deputy of the Riga City Council has said.
On September 22, the Lithuanian Seimas approved lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons within the country. Following a discussion of the issue, the parliament referred a constitutional amendment to the relevant committees for review.
"There is a vast, if not enormous, gap between repealing Article 137 and the actual arrival of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian soil. Decisions to deploy nuclear warheads would require specific consent from the US and NATO, military infrastructure, specialized security and storage procedures, and would entail significant political costs," Pankratov said.
In his opinion, such decisions amount to an "ostentatious demonstration of Lithuania's readiness for the closest possible military-political integration with NATO."
Pankratov also emphasized that the practical value of deploying nuclear warheads in Lithuania for NATO is quite limited.
"The alliance is unlikely to rush the deployment of nuclear weapons right on the Russian and Belarusian borders, as this would sharply increase the risk of actual - rather than merely rhetorical - escalation for its domestic electorate," he explained.

The workers were sorting vegetables inside the facility when it was hit, according to Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi.
