articles.title: The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
articles.body:
The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
The inaugural summit of the new Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation format, initiated by Ukraine with EU support, took place on September 18-20. Leaders and representatives from eight countries in the Carpathian region were invited to discuss security, energy, logistics, and cross-border cooperation. The initiative – intended to unite nations, some of which do not officially supply weapons to Ukraine but wish to foster “good-neighborly relations” – has turned into a zero-sum game. Yielding no significant economic benefits and failing to address real economic challenges, it only serves to isolate the region from pan-continental logistics corridors.
Is the Carpathian Initiative a Ukrainian or European project?
The foundation for the Carpathian Initiative was laid by Ukraine back in 2001-2003, when it acted as the primary initiator and depositary of the Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians. Initially, the format was strictly environmental and conservation-oriented. Countries of the Visegrad Group, and primarily Poland, breathed geopolitical life and economic scale into the concept. For years, Warsaw actively advocated for the creation of a full-fledged EU Macro-Regional Strategy for the Carpathian Region (EUSCARP), aiming to transform the shared mountain range into a major logistics and infrastructure hub.
Over time, the EU fully took over this regional initiative, turning it into a systemic tool for the “soft integration” of Ukraine. After developing a strategic vision for the region in 2009 and adopting the Carpathian Roadmap in 2019, Brussels institutionalized the project in line with its own bureaucratic standards. What began as a modest environmental initiative has, through the efforts of European neighbors, transformed into a large-scale EU geopolitical project aimed at drawing Ukraine into the European orbit via infrastructure grants.
The September summit marked the latest stage of this project. Ukraine (backed by EU funding) attempted to reclaim its role as the primary “driving force” of the whole initiative by shifting the focus from environmental issues to matters essential for bolstering Ukraine’s influence on NATO’s eastern flank.
Ukraine’s autonomy is illusory, however. For the European Commission, the Carpathian region serves as a convenient geographic ‘sandbox’; the supranational bureaucracy seeks to bind the EU’s eastern fringes together through mutual dependency. Brussels’ ultimate goal is to dilute the agency and curb the independence of countries like Hungary and Slovakia, whose ‘Eastern’ initiatives – such as linking Central and Eastern Europe with Greater Eurasia – are gaining momentum. Ultimately, this measure would allow regional financial and other flows to be fully contained within the EU.
What’s wrong with the project, and why is it a zero-sum game?
Beneath the facade of discussions on “cross-border cooperation” set against the picturesque backdrop of the Ukrainian Carpathians lie pragmatic objectives that turn the Carpathian Eight into a classic zero-sum game. This is confirmed by the project’s geography: countries with the greatest interest in the initiative find themselves subordinate to those countries for whom the project is not a key priority. Ukraine’s actual geographic weight in the project is minimal; despite Kiev’s ambition to act as the main engine of regional integration, the Carpathians account for a mere 3.6% of Ukraine’s total territory. Ukraine possesses only 10% of the total area of the mountain range, yet it attempts to dictate the agenda to Romania and Slovakia, where the Carpathians form the backbone of national geography, covering 47% and 72% of the territory, respectively. Such evident disparity between Ukraine’s actual geographical “contribution” and its political ambitions sows the seeds of conflict within the project.
Moreover, the Carpathian macroregion is considered depressed and heterogeneous. Unlike the economically developed, navigable, and homogeneous Danube region – which served as a model for this project conceived by the Visegrad Group – the Carpathians are a patchwork of isolated mountainous areas. For centuries, this 190,000 sq km area has remained a remote periphery. Due to the highly underdeveloped infrastructure – the lack of modern roads, tunnels, and logistics hubs – the border regions of these eight countries have been trapped in a state of deprivation. In the past 25 years, no amount of targeted European funding has been able to rectify this situation. This should have compelled Brussels to step out of its comfort zone and realistically assess the physical boundaries of the region. This also explains why the Visegrad Group supports eastern initiatives in Greater Eurasia. However, instead of this, along with the economically unfeasible Three Seas Initiative and the “frontline zones” project, the Carpathians are being turned into another logistical dead end resembling an artificial buffer zone.
This perspective reveals the true purpose of the revived format: to serve as a covert logistical corridor for NATO. The projected budget of €9.4 billion ($10.7 billion) for 90 infrastructure projects is specifically aimed at modernizing narrow-gauge railways, bridges, and tunnels in the Carpathian Mountains. Under the guise of Euro-integration, Brussels is aggressively attempting to create a secure alternative route through the complex mountainous terrain for rapid deployment of heavy equipment, weapons, and NATO reserves, bypassing vulnerable border logistics nodes. Consequently, supranational strategists get to fully benefit from this venture while Central European countries bear all the attendant military and strategic risks.
Intrigues, scandals, and investigations
For the countries physically located in the Carpathians and those interested in developing the region, the hidden agenda of the initiative is apparent. Citing a sudden illness, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico canceled his visit to Bukovel and expressed his outright opposition to turning the region into a frontline zone and dragging Bratislava into the conflict under the guise of NATO obligations. As a result, Slovakia was represented at the summit only by the state secretary for foreign and European affairs. Local experts openly stated that Bratislava guessed the proposed zero-sum game: under the guise of cross-border corridors, Brussels and Kiev are attempting to establish a rear hub for supplying NATO’s eastern flank. For Slovakia, participating in such “road modernization” carries direct military risks, not security benefits. This forces the country to navigate a precarious line – seeking economic grants while sabotaging the military-political agenda of the proposed C8.
Following Slovakia, the Czech Republic demonstrated passive resistance to the project by adopting a stance of cautious pragmatism. Unlike Warsaw, Prague notably refrained from sending top officials to Bukovel, opting instead to send the vice-president of the senate. Czech economic analysts expressed doubt about the €40 billion investment portfolio announced by Kiev. The most important indicator of the failure of the “unified front” was that the Czech Republic effectively refused to sign the summit’s final declaration. As regional analysts point out, the country has “cooled” towards Ukraine’s ambitions. Moreover, unlike Ukraine, the Czech Republic has a realistic grasp of its geography; possessing only 8.5% of Carpathian territory, Prague saw no tangible economic benefit in a project burdened with militarization issues rather than cross-border development. Consequently, it chose to remain on the sidelines, unwilling to endorse someone else’s frontline agenda.
Predictably, only Poland and Romania expressed full and unconditional support for the project, emerging as the principal political beneficiaries of the initiative. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Romanian President Nicusor Dan signed the final declaration, explicitly linking it to military-strategic objectives. For Warsaw, the Carpathian Eight provided a convenient platform for lobbying an anti-ballistic missile defense coalition on NATO’s eastern flank, while for Bucharest, it offered a means to logistically connect the Ukrainian border with NATO’s largest European base, which is being constructed on Romanian territory. As a result, the document was signed only by those players intending to gain direct benefits from the region’s militarization, firmly establishing the C8 as a frontline coalition.
Hungary’s reaction is particularly noteworthy. On X, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar compared Kiev’s actions to village sports: “Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrey Sibiga, expressed surprise over Hungary’s attitude, but the situation is very clear and leaves no room for doubt.
Budapest was expected to sign the memorandum between its oil and gas company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz to establish joint strategic fuel reserves along the border. However, Magyar firmly blocked this initiative, fully aware of the risks involved in turning Hungary’s bordering territories with oil depots into targets for someone else’s military needs. Apparently, even Euro-Atlantic solidarity has its physical boundaries.
Moreover, Budapest’s negative stance is reinforced by the situation in Transcarpathia. From 2014, the Hungarian population in the region has decreased from 150,000 people to around 70,000-80,000 due to stringent Ukrainianization policies in schools. The remaining population is facing selective forced conscription, with military recruitment offices compiling lists of Hungarian students and workers to send to the front lines, resulting in several widely reported casualties, including the death of 45-year-old Jozsef Sebestyen. Notably, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry is closely monitoring these developments: mobilized residents of Transcarpathia occasionally end up as prisoners of war, and Russian diplomatic agencies, in coordination with intelligence services, work on their direct transfer to Hungary, bypassing Ukraine. Aware that Brussels and Kiev are attempting to exploit Hungarian resources and territory, Magyar chose to flip the script. Budapest refused to fund this military version of ‘Carpathian soccer’ which is too costly for it, and vetoed Ukraine’s integration efforts.
In summary, we must note that despite the ambitions of European supranational entities to create artificial buffer zones (essentially ‘sandboxes’) in Central and Eastern Europe, their era is coming to an end. Attempts to impose a zero-sum game on other countries only exacerbate the internal rift which is becoming inevitable, considering the region’s actual geography and the projects gaining momentum across Greater Eurasia.

articles.title: CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft in volume as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work.
General Atomics announced earlier this week it has the capacity to produce its FQ-42A Vengeance drones at a rate of “six aircraft per month to meet USAF goals” and could make more if needed. Competitor Anduril, which started production of its FQ-44A Fury at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio in March, aims to build 150 aircraft annually, its officials said last week at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
The Air Force’s 2027 budget request includes $996.5 million to acquire production CCAs in fiscal 2027, plus another $150 million in advance procurement funds for 2028. But USAF has not specified how many aircraft that might cover.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer.
Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42.
General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026.
GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities.
The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026.
General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July.
The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.”
Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace.
The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings.
The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay.
General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
“The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”

articles.title: US Company That Sold Software To Pentagon, Secret Service Lied About Russian Ownership, Officials Say
articles.body:
A US company that provided digital forensics and data-extraction software to the Pentagon and other government agencies was in fact owned by a Russian company that also sold software to Russian spy agencies, US authorities charged.
Oxygen Forensics' chief executive -- Lee Reiber, 55, of Idaho -- was arrested on wire fraud and released on bail on September 22, US prosecutors said. A Russian man -- Oleg Davydov, 52, of Moscow – was arrested at London’s Heathrow Airport two days earlier, and US officials said they will seek his extradition.
In the indictment released on September 23, US prosecutors said Oxygen Forensics -- and Reiber in particular -- allegedly told the US government that the Virginia-registered company had no foreign ownership or control and that its software was developed in the United States.
In fact, prosecutors alleged, Oxygen Forensics was owned by Davydov and four other unnamed Russian citizens who also ran a Moscow-based company that provides software services to the Federal Security Services, Russia’s main intelligence agency.
The company set up a US affiliate in the suburbs of Washington, D.C. in 2013.
After 2022, when the United States and other Western countries tightened regulations in the wake of Moscow’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Davydov and his partners allegedly moved to conceal Oxygen Forensics’ ownership.
Inside Russia, Oxygen was renamed MKO Systems. The company's main application -- called Mobile Forensic Detective -- is in wide use among Russian law enforcement agencies.
The software that Oxygen provided to US government agencies was data-extraction software, used to circumvent security features and gather data from mobile phones, computers, and other electronic devices.
The National Computer Forensics Institute for the Secret Service -- the agency that provides protective details to the White House and government officials -- signed a five-year contract with the company in 2024.
"The complaint does not allege that the software contained malicious code or that it was used to gain unauthorized access to any customer’s computer systems or data," authorities said.
Both Reiber and Davydov were charged with wire fraud. Reiber did not immediately respond to an e-mail seeking comment. Davydov could not be located for comment.
The announcement comes as hacking, cyberespionage, malware, and other malicious computer activities has exploded in use around the world.
Government agencies -- Russian, US, Chinese, Israeli, and Iranian -- have invested massive sums into building out new cybercapabilities, and private companies increasingly have access to powerful new nongovernment tools.
The FBI on September 23 announced it was investigating a claim that a hacker group had stolen sensitive files belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website.

articles.title: Russians guard Madagascar’s parliament speaker as Moscow builds Indian Ocean foothold – RFE/RL
articles.body:
Since Madagascar’s October 2025 coup, Russian military personnel have joined the parliament speaker’s security detail, and Russian instructors have begun training Malagasy soldiers, RFE/RL reported. OSINT investigators traced a flight carrying a senior Russian military intelligence officer and 40 of Russia's Africa Corps members to the island on 20 December 2025.
Madagascar’s new leadership has welcomed Russian military assistance, while Moscow has pursued media projects, energy talks, and the possible recruitment of Malagasy workers. RFE/RL says the prospective destination is Alabuga, a plant producing drones used against Ukraine. Elsewhere in Africa, Russia has sent troops, sought access to resources, and opened cultural centers.
Major General Andrei Averyanov, who oversees Russian military intelligence operations in Africa, was on the December flight. He traveled with members of Africa Corps, a Russian Defense Ministry unit that absorbed some Wagner forces. Madagascar's National Assembly speaker Siteny Randrianasoloniaiko announced the unit’s arrival that month.
Russian intelligence officer Anton Papshev attended the January launch of training for Madagascar’s 1st Airborne Battalion. The program also included a transfer of Russian weapons, though RFE/RL did not specify which ones. In February, interim President Michael Randrianirina met Vladimir Putin in Moscow and welcomed wider cooperation on defense, energy, and other areas.
Russian authorities signed a deal with Randrianasoloniaiko to open a Russia House, a Kremlin cultural center. Ukraine’s military intelligence said Moscow plans to expand the network across Africa to influence young people. Madagascar also authorized a branch of African Initiative, a Russia-linked media organization that helped National Radio launch a “Russ-Mada” program.
RFE/RL said Russian authorities appear to intend to recruit Malagasy workers for Alabuga, a drone assembly plant in Russia’s Tatarstan region.
The plant has recruited thousands of workers, mainly young women from Africa and Central and South Asia, for relatively high-paying jobs. Richard Rakotonirina, head of Madagascar’s Friends of Russia association, visited Alabuga in February. RFE/RL did not establish that any Malagasy workers had been recruited.
Moscow recruits African women to produce drones in horrific conditions — investigation exposes large-scale fraud
During a visit to Moscow, Madagascar’s prime minister discussed Russian fuel supplies, oil storage on the island, and military training.
A Russian delegation also visited an abandoned naval base that Madagascar and France had already agreed to study restoring. RFE/RL did not report any agreement giving Russia access to the base.
Russia’s wider reach in Africa
Madagascar’s emerging ties resemble security arrangements Moscow has built elsewhere in Africa. In the Central African Republic, Russian mercenaries guarded officials and trained troops in exchange for access to gold, diamonds, and timber, RFE/RL reported. Russia's Africa Corps protects the Republic of the Congo’s president, Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled since 1979, apart from a brief interruption.
In Mali, the force backs a military government and has deployed a drone of a type developed for Russia’s war against Ukraine. Residents and a rights group told RFI that Russian and Malian forces killed four civilian herders. Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting forces fighting Russian troops there.

articles.title: Kiev deliberately destabilizing global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
articles.body:
Kiev deliberately destabilizing global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
Ukraine’s deliberate attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure are destabilizing global markets, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Lavrov and Rubio met on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, where they held an extensive discussion on Ukraine, bilateral relations, and a range of international issues.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Lavrov drew Rubio’s attention to what it described as close coordination between Kiev and its European backers and raised Ukrainian strikes on civilians and “cross-border infrastructure facilities,” which Russia said are deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
The issue has increasingly drawn attention in Washington as diesel prices have surged to record highs, topping $6.50 a gallon nationally in September 2026. US President Donald Trump recently urged Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky to stop striking Russian refineries, saying the attacks were creating a global shortage and “hurting the world.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent similarly said earlier this month that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products were contributing to an “energy shock.”
The US State Department’s brief readout from the Lavrov-Rubio meeting on Wednesday said only that the two diplomats had discussed the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the US-Russia relationship.
Following the meeting, Rubio said both Russia and Ukraine had expressed some interest in a limited ceasefire covering energy targets. He acknowledged, however, that such an arrangement “doesn’t solve the war,” and said reaching one would be difficult because both sides regard energy infrastructure as a strategic target.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected the idea that any limited truce can substitute for a comprehensive settlement, pointing to what it describes as Ukraine’s past violations of ceasefires and arguing that Kiev seeks talks only when the situation on the battlefield becomes critical. Zelensky said this week that Kiev was prepared to stop targeting Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on a wide range of Ukraine’s energy, logistics, and port infrastructure.
Lavrov reiterated on Wednesday that Russia would not halt its military operation merely to facilitate negotiations, arguing that such a pause would give Kiev and its European sponsors time to replenish depleted weapons stocks.
Zelensky has meanwhile continued to push for the “full and swift implementation” of the recently enacted sanctions package championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham. The law gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, potentially targeting countries such as China and India. With global supplies already strained, sharply curbing Russian exports could further disrupt energy trade and drive prices higher as major importers are forced to compete for alternative barrels.
The Russian side reiterated during the Rubio talks that it remains prepared to pursue a political and diplomatic settlement, but only one that addresses the “root causes” of the conflict. Russian officials have repeatedly identified NATO’s expansion toward Russia and Kiev’s policies toward Russian speakers among those issues.
Lavrov also called for further normalization of US-Russia relations, including resolving disputes over diplomatic missions and Russian diplomatic property in the US.
In another sign of continued engagement, Rubio announced after the talks that Washington had invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December. The Kremlin welcomed the invitation and said it would consider it through diplomatic channels.

articles.title: United Kingdom Established a Unit to Protect Satellites
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force has established the No. III Space Effects Squadron, which is the country’s first unit dedicated to countering threats to British satellites.
Air Chief Marshal Harv Smith, Chief of the Air Staff, announced the unit’s creation at the UK Space Capabilities Conference, according to the country’s Ministry of Defense.
The new squadron will bring together specialists from various branches of the Armed Forces to counter hostile activities in orbit and protect satellite infrastructure.
Unlike the 1st and 2nd Squadrons, which handle surveillance and early warning, the 3rd Squadron will use electronic warfare capabilities to neutralize threats.
The newly formed unit will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand as new technologies become available.
In 2025, General Paul Tedman, head of Space Command, reported that Russia attempts to interfere with British military satellites on a weekly basis—both through ground-based jamming and by maneuvering its own spacecraft close to the United Kingdom’s orbital systems.
He emphasized that Russia and China have tested anti-satellite weapons and are also exploring the possibility of deploying nuclear weapons in space.

articles.title: Denmark predicts an expansion of the scale of Russia’s hybrid warfare
articles.body:
Denmark predicts an expansion of the scale of Russia’s hybrid warfare
Kyiv • UNN
Danish intelligence expects more frequent and dangerous cyberattacks and acts of sabotage by Russia against the West and NATO. The risk of a limited attack is increasing.
Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service predicts that Russia will expand the scale of its hybrid warfare against Western countries. This is stated in a new threat assessment, reports UNN.
The security situation has deteriorated further. Russia has intensified its use of sabotage, destructive cyberattacks and drone attacks against targets in Europe. Hybrid warfare is gaining momentum. This concerns, for example, the thwarted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, which, according to German authorities, had been planned in Russia for several months. Russia has become more willing to take risks. Russian drones, and in some cases even missiles, have been shot down in NATO countries bordering Ukraine
The intelligence service expects Russia to escalate its hybrid warfare even further.
Until now, Russia has primarily carried out hybrid attacks against targets in the West in order to sow fear and reduce public support for Ukraine. Russia has increasingly sought to directly disrupt the delivery of this support, for example by sabotaging defence industry facilities or railways used to transport military equipment to Ukraine. The intelligence service assesses that in the coming months Russia will intensify its hybrid warfare even further, carrying out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO that will have more serious consequences for the affected countries than before. This could, for example, include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for vital societal functions and sabotage attacks carrying a high risk of casualties
The intelligence service also noted that there is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. This could happen even if Russia continues its war against Ukraine and does not develop the necessary capabilities to wage a regional war.
A limited military attack would be a desperate step on Russia’s part and, like the escalation of hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months. The aim of such an attack would be to divert European resources from supporting Ukraine and divide NATO if the alliance is unable to agree on a joint response
The intelligence service predicts that a limited military attack could, for example, take the form of isolated Russian long-range strikes against infrastructure that plays an important role in providing support to Ukraine. Russia could subsequently claim that the missiles struck NATO territory exclusively because their trajectory had been altered by Ukraine. It could also involve a so-called “false flag” operation, in which Russia, for example, uses Ukrainian-made drones to attack a NATO country.
We remind you
Russia has launched a new wave of attacks on European weapons manufacturing plants under the guise of plausible deniability.

articles.title: Four "Zircon" missiles and three ballistic missiles were neutralized over Ukraine during Russia's massive attack
articles.body:
Four "Zircon" missiles and three ballistic missiles were neutralized over Ukraine during Russia's massive attack
Kyiv • UNN
At night, Russia launched 282 drones and missiles at Ukraine, including "Zircon" missiles and ballistic missiles. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 227 targets.
Russia struck Ukraine with missiles, including "Zircon" missiles and ballistic missiles, and 282 drones during the night of September 24; 4 "Zircons," 3 ballistic missiles, and 220 drones, including a "Banderol," were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 24 (starting at 18:00 on September 23), the enemy attacked with Zircon anti-ship missiles from the Kursk, Rostov, and Oryol regions of the Russian Federation; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from the Kursk and Bryansk regions of the Russian Federation; 282 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs, Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; Hvardiyske, Chauda — the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea; and the waters of the Sea of Azov.
Where the enemy struck
"The main areas targeted were the Odesa and Kyiv regions," the statement said.
How air defense performed
The air assault was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had shot down/suppressed 227 targets:
-  4 Zircon anti-ship missiles; 
-  3 Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles; 
-  1 "Banderol"/"Dan-T"; 
-  219 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types, as well as drones of other types.

articles.title: Zelensky in New York discusses Patriot interceptors, winter support package with Rutte

Zelensky in New York discusses Patriot interceptors, winter support package with Rutte

“When we met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Kyiv had already been hit by three waves of ballistic attacks. I briefed Mark in detail on all the consequences: the destruction and the casualties. This is the constant reality Ukraine is living with. It is impossible to counter this terror against life on your own,” Zelensky said.
He noted that Ukrainians had learned to intercept cruise missiles and drones, while work was continuing to find a solution against jet-powered Shahed drones, with “good results” already achieved.
“But against ballistic missiles, for now, the only effective option is Patriot interceptors, which we need practically every day. We discussed our needs for these interceptors and how we can secure a winter support package. Thank you, Mark, for your readiness to look for solutions. This is very important for NATO member states as well, given Russia’s constant threats to go further and destroy the lives of other nations,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky previously said that one of the key elements in strengthening Ukraine’s overall position should be a winter package of air defense missiles, including 100 Patriot missiles per month, or 300 missiles for the winter.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s need for protection against ballistic missiles already exceeds its available capabilities. Ukraine and its European partners are therefore working on the joint FREYJA anti-ballistic system, which could become operational within a year.

articles.title: US Navy admits suicide attempts on carrier strike group
articles.body:
US Navy admits suicide attempts on carrier strike group
Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a ten-month deployment that included the country’s war against Iran, CNN reported on Thursday, citing a letter from the service’s acting secretary.
The carrier, whose tour of duty began in late November 2025, drew media attention earlier this year after reports emerged of logistical and maintenance problems, including food and basic-supply shortages, a lack of hot and potable water, and plumbing failures.
In a written response to questions from Senator Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao disclosed the figure, which hadn’t previously been made public and covers several ships that travel together, including the carrier. Cao also noted that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment that was expected to end in May but has been extended indefinitely.
In August, military outlets Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported, citing crew members’ families, that collapsing morale, burnout, and mental health problems had driven several sailors to attempt to jump overboard.
The Pentagon has moved to dismiss senior editorial staff at Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination, after the outlet reported on US military operations in the Middle East, including problems involving weapons supplies and the extended deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln. The moves came after senior staff publicly opposed potential Pentagon interference in the outlet’s editorial independence.
Last month, multiple media outlets cited officials as saying that the aircraft carrier was finally heading home from its extended deployment. Earlier this week, Military Times reported that the ship and Carrier Strike Group 3 pulled into Guam for a short logistics stop, officially marking the tenth month of its tour of duty.
The confirmation of suicide attempts previously disclosed by the media comes ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, amid mounting public disapproval of the Iran war.
Earlier this week, a poll conducted by SSRS for CNN suggested that Americans’ opposition to the war in the Islamic Republic had hardened, with nearly two-thirds saying the US is not winning the conflict and an even larger share saying President Donald Trump is not doing enough to end it. Last week, a Fox News national survey found that 71% of respondents believe the current administration lacks a plan to end the war, while 60% called the military action against the Islamic Republic the “wrong decision.”
Trump, along with members of his administration, has repeatedly accused media outlets of spreading “fake news” about various issues related to the Iran war, including reports that US weapons stockpiles have been depleted.

articles.body:
A Russian overnight attack on Odesa damaged a medical facility, 10 residential buildings and a school, local authorities said on Sept. 24.
The strike damaged the roof and part of the upper floor of the medical facility, while blast waves shattered windows in nearby homes and the school.

No casualties were reported in the preliminary assessment.
Municipal workers began clearing the area overnight. The street has since been cleared, while damaged windows in residential buildings have been boarded up.
Residents are receiving assistance with applications for compensation under Ukraine’s state eVidnovlennia program and Odesa’s Unbreakable Odesa initiative.
Odesa has faced a sustained wave of Russian missile and drone attacks in recent weeks, with strikes hitting residential buildings, logistics facilities, energy infrastructure, warehouses and the city’s port.
On Sept. 23, a Russian attack hit a foreign-flagged commercial cargo ship in the Odesa region, killing its Ukrainian captain. The same attack also set fire to warehouses storing medicines, household goods and food.
Two days earlier, on Sept. 21, Russian forces struck warehouses storing food products for supermarket chains near Odesa, triggering a major fire. More than 80 rescuers were involved in extinguishing the blaze.
On Sept. 19, Russia again struck an 11-story administrative building in Odesa that had been hit the previous day, setting its upper floors on fire. A two-story educational building was also damaged, while two private homes and vehicles were damaged in Odesa district. The attack also hit energy facilities, leaving more than 178,000 households without power.

It also said that the roof of a seven-story city hospital building and a 10-story non-residential building were damaged.

Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.

articles.title: How the U.K. Is Supporting Saudi Arabia In Its Fight Against the Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia will have assistance from a key Western ally in its fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, as Britain is providing military support to the Kingdom in a bid to help restore stability in the region and ease pressures on the global energy supply.
“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb, a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices.
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
How exactly will the U.K. be supporting Saudi Arabia?
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year, and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The long-standing alliance between the U.K. and Saudi Arabia
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre, the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
How are Saudi Arabia’s other allies responding to the Houthis' advances?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France, Pakistan, and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
Trump is understood to have received requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to strike the Houthi rebels. According to the New York Times, Trump reportedly considered launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend, before ultimately deciding against it. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Asked Tuesday why Washington has held back from striking the Houthis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it’s “a very dangerous and complex” conflict.
“If it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so,” he said, referencing the U.S. economic and defense partnership with Saudi Arabia signed last November, that deepened co-operation between the two countries.
Fears mount over global energy supply as Houthis advance
Global energy supplies have been under increasing strain since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28, as Tehran has leveraged its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed prior to the conflict.
In the past few weeks, the Houthis have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha and the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. If the Houthis were to assume control of the strait, shipping companies could be forced to travel via South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope—a longer, costlier route.
The volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through the Bab el-Mandeb increased earlier this year, with the route being used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The shipments surged from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
However, recent crossings have been marred by uncertainty over the potential threat posed by the Houthis. Data shared with TIME by Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, showed an estimated 34 vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on Sept. 15, a drop from the estimated 53 crossings recorded on July 15th.
A spokesperson for the Houthis on Sept. 11 insisted the waterway will remain free to roam “with the exception of Saudi ships.” Yet concerns among global leaders and shipping companies remain.
Burnham and other U.K. officials have framed Britain’s defensive support partly around the potential economic consequences at home. The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025, according to data from the Office of National Statistics.
Wearing says that because oil is traded on a global market, supply disruptions in one region can push up benchmark prices worldwide, with those costs cascading through the broader economy.
“What Americans call gas and what we call petrol, if that goes up, think how many goods to market are taken by heavy lorries on petrol. It can push up the price of everything: shipping, road transit, energy, all kinds of industrial production and many consumer products,” he says. “Oil is the lifeblood of the world economy, the longer you restrict the supply, the higher the price goes, the more inflationary pressure there is on everything, and that affects Britain, but it affects the whole system. It's like a heart attack in a human body, suddenly it's not being pumped round."

articles.title: Poland says Starlink fire was sabotage
articles.body:
The fire at a Starlink ground station near Warsaw on Wednesday night was an act of sabotage and part of hybrid warfare against Poland, Digital Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Thursday morning.
“[This was] sabotage and an attempt to disrupt the operation of a vital station that is crucial for the security and continuity of internet services in Ukraine,” Gawkowski told state broadcaster TVP Info, stopping short of blaming Russia for the incident directly.
“It’s about actions aimed at shutting down the internet and disrupting the functioning of basic services. These may concern the supply of water, gas or electricity, as well as the financial system,” Gawkowski added.
Advertisement
The fire broke out in the village of Wola Krobowska, 50 kilometers south of Warsaw. It didn’t cause significant damage and there were no injuries. Poland’s counterintelligence agency, ABW, and the police are investigating the incident.
Operated by the state-owned telecoms company Exatel, the station links Starlink satellites to terrestrial internet networks. Together with a station in Kaunas, Lithuania, it serves Central European users as well as Ukraine, Polish media reported.
The minister has previously warned that Poland faces some 2,000–3,000 cyberattacks on its infrastructure daily.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that NATO, Ukrainian and Polish intelligence assessments point to Russian plans to step up hybrid attacks on countries supporting Kyiv, including Poland, in the coming months.
Tusk also said Moscow would mask such strikes as accidents to undermine NATO’s willingness to respond collectively.
Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski urged Moscow to end the war at the U.N. Security Council Wednesday, citing the West’s economic superiority over Russia.
“You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win. You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time,” Sikorski said.

articles.title: No pause in Ukraine conflict for peace talks – Lavrov
articles.body:
No pause in Ukraine conflict for peace talks – Lavrov
Moscow will not pause its special military operation while peace negotiations are underway, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday, asserting that a temporary ceasefire only benefits Kiev.
Ukraine and 51 of its allies released a statement on Wednesday demanding that Russia accept an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire” so that peace talks between Moscow and Kiev can take place. The statement, whose signatories included the EU and its member states, the UK, Canada, and Australia, was published before the security council met to discuss the conflict.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov said during the meeting. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
Kiev is “clearly and blatantly using terrorist methods,” Lavrov added, referring to Ukraine’s long-range strikes on civilian targets in Russia.
Ukraine and its allies issued their ceasefire demand less than four days after Ukrainian forces launched their largest-ever drone raid on the Russian capital. The attack killed two civilians in its suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the “unprecedented” raid involved more than 1,600 UAVs from all directions.
Throughout the conflict, Ukraine has repeatedly followed such attacks with appeals for ceasefire, which Russia has rebuffed. Moscow maintains that it will only cease military action when both sides seek a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict.
Russia has dramatically stepped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian military and dual-use infrastructure in recent months, in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day “influence campaign” of long-range strikes on civilian targets.
Zelensky’s stated aim was to foment discontent among the Russian public, but the campaign ultimately ended with the destruction of Ukraine’s Black Sea port infrastructure and an earlier-than-usual start to Russia’s winter campaign against its power plants and substations.
In a statement released after the latest drone raid on Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said that the Russian army would further “intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kiev” in response.

articles.title: US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
articles.body:
US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Iranian airlines are being cut off from international routes and airport services as Washington steps up pressure on the country’s aviation sector. Several regional connections have already been suspended or restricted, although some foreign flights continue, RT’s Saman Kojouri has reported from outside the Tehran headquarters of Mahan Air, one of Iran’s major carriers.
The US Treasury targeted 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month as part of a broader campaign against the country’s aviation sector. Foreign companies providing services to the carriers risk US secondary sanctions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the restrictions would effectively shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation from September 23.
”If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.
The impact is already spreading across the region, according to RT’s Kojouri. Azerbaijan has suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers, while Iraq has reportedly stopped accepting Iranian aircraft. Flights between Tehran and Muscat have also been suspended, while Georgia has said it will comply with sanctions affecting Iranian carriers.
Mahan Air is among the airlines facing the squeeze. Washington first sanctioned the carrier in 2011, accusing it of providing support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF). The Treasury has since targeted companies abroad accused of providing commercial and logistical support to the airline.
The aviation crackdown comes as Washington ramps up pressure on Tehran while simultaneously pursuing diplomatic contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. President Donald Trump threatened on Tuesday to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if negotiations fail, saying he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement and further military escalation.
Most of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall during Trump’s speech, leaving only one representative seated. The US president defended the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war and accused Tehran of pursuing nuclear weapons and supporting terrorism.
Despite the hostile rhetoric, indirect contacts continued later in the day. US envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had shuttled between the American and Iranian delegations during “lengthy talks,” while Tehran said it had used the channel to clearly convey its conditions to Washington, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 16, injure 59 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by waves of drones, ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 16, injure 59 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by waves of drones, ballistic missiles
At least 16 people were killed and 59 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia launched several waves of ballistic missiles at Kyiv overnight, local authorities said on Sept. 24.
Two people were killed and eight others injured in Kyiv, where Russian ballistic missiles struck the capital in three waves overnight. Residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy, and logistics infrastructure were among the sites damaged, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"Every such attack happens because pressure on the aggressor has still not become total, and Russia believes it can continue relying on ballistic terror," Zelensky said. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives."
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
In Donetsk Oblast, eight people were killed and 19 others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Five people were killed in Oleksandrivka, two in Kramatorsk, and one in Sloviansk.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed six people and injured 12 others over the past day, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Among the attacks, Russia struck an agricultural enterprise in Stara Hnylytsia, where 12 people were injured, according to the Governor.
In Sumy Oblast, nine people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out nearly 60 attacks against 22 settlements.
In Odesa Oblast, two people were injured in a mass combined Russian attack that damaged a hospital, a school, residential buildings, a shopping center, warehouses, and other civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were injured as Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, local authorities said. Two apartment buildings, a house and gas pipelines were damaged.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 690 strikes against 55 settlements across the region over the past day.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured one person over the past day, regional authorities said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones and artillery.

articles.title: Ukraine transfers two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," said Zelensky in his speech.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die."
Zelensky did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January last year.
They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country entered the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelensky said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced.
South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea's unification and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Zelensky criticizes North Korea's military support for Russia
Zelensky in his speech also criticized North Korea for sending its troops to fight for Russia.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent around 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia's war against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates.
Most of them have been deployed in the Russian region of Kursk, where they helped Moscow's forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The country has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

articles.title: No breakthrough for US-Iran talks despite flurry of diplomacy
articles.body:
At the UN, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian rebuked US threats, stating that anyone attempting to bully the nation must understand that it is "ready for dialogue, diplomacy, and negotiations without accepting the language of force." Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that an Iran deal requires prolonged effort, but military options remain available
Iran-backed Houthis are continuing their advance with the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen
Israel continues to attack the Gaza Strip, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
And so we begin our live coverage of the day...
US-seized tankers of Iranian oil are in Atlantic: tracker
Three Iran-linked oil tankers seized by the United States and carrying nearly six million barrels of Iranian crude oil were in the Atlantic Ocean on Thursday, tracking data indicated.
They did not have their destination marked on their transponders, but specialist website TankerTrackers said Wednesday on X that they were heading towards the United States.
"Nearly six million barrels (valued at nearly $600 million) of seized Iranian crude oil are quietly crossing the Atlantic Ocean towards the United States of America," the post said.
One of the tankers, the Majestic X, briefly listed the US as its destination from July 31 to August 2, as it began heading towards the Atlantic from waters off Malaysia, according to tracking data from maritime platform Kpler.
The three tankers are sanctioned by the United States under programmes aimed at limiting Iran's oil exports.
They were seized after the US started a blockade of Iranian ports in retaliation for Iran's closing of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil exports from Gulf countries.
Iranian and Ukrainian foreign ministers meet in New York
The Iranian and Ukrainian foreign ministers held a meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, the semi-official Mehr news agency reported, the first such meeting since tensions rose in July following a Ukrainian attack on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea.
Iraq is exporting around 2.6 million barrels of oil per day from its southern ports so far in September and producing more than 3 million bpd from its southern oilfields, Bassem Abdul Karim, head of Iraq's Basra Oil Company, said on Thursday.
Abdul Karim, speaking at an energy conference in Basra, added that Iraq is transporting around 250,000 bpd of Basra crude to Kirkuk for exports via Ceyhan in Turkey.
On September 16, Iraq launched a pilot operation to transport crude oil by road from its southern oilfields to a Kirkuk storage facility in an effort to boost supplies to the northern export system and potentially increase shipments through Turkey's Ceyhan port.
The initiative forms part of broader Iraqi efforts toincrease flows through the northern export route after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted Iraq's shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, its main export route.
Saudi coalition: intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said Thursday that its forces intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Iran-backed group, thwarting attacks on the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu.
"Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly," said coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki in a series of posts on X.
The Houthis have advanced in Yemen over the past week. [Getty]
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers".
The Israeli prime minister's brief stay in New York for his speech at the UN General Assembly includes meetings with several world leaders, according to his office—but not Trump, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio or any Arab leaders.
Netanyahu's office claimed "many world leaders" asked to meet with Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but that he was on a "tight schedule" and needed to return to Israel before the start of the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, which begins at sundown on Friday.
Netanyahu will meet with the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Panama, and Ethiopia, the vice president of Colombia, and the prime ministers of Greece, Slovenia, and Papua New Guinea, according to his office.
EU says only a fraction of needed Gaza funds collected
A top EU official says only 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) has been raised out of the 71 billion euros ($80.8 billion) that the United Nations, the World Bank and the 27-nation European Union estimate are needed to rebuild Gaza.
“All of us, we have to scale up our efforts,” said European Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica, speaking on the sidelines of the General Assembly. She called for a unified recovery plan that would bring together Israel, the Palestinian Authority, the U.S.-backed Board of Peace, and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
UN rights chief 'appalled' by Yemen conflict's swelling toll
The UN rights chief is "appalled" by the growing civilian toll in the Yemen conflict, his office said Thursday, with at least 125 civilians killed and wounded in attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis since the start of August.
"As if the people of Yemen haven't already endured enough misery, civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said in a statement, insisting that "civilians must never be targeted, and their protection must be the overriding priority".
Yemen govt forces repel Houthi push on key Taiz-Aden route
Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces repelled overnight attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on a key supply route to the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, government sources said on Thursday.
The steep, winding mountain pass, known as Hejat al-Abd, is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas.
The Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
German institutes double GDP forecasts amid Iran war turmoil
Leading German think-tanks on Thursday more than doubled their 2026 growth forecast for Europe's biggest economy as it withstands the Iran war energy shock, but warned of risks from rising debt levels.
The economy is now expected to expand 1.3 percent this year, up from a forecast of 0.6 percent in April, the five economic institutes said in a statement.
They also raised their prediction for 2027 slightly to 1.1 percent.
"The German economy performed significantly better in the first half of 2026 than had been expected in spring," they said, with growth supported by strong exports and a robust manufacturing sector.
"Although the energy price shock associated with the Iran war has weighed on the German economy, the higher prices for motor fuels and heating oil have so far had little spillover effect on broader consumer prices," they added.
Business rivals in the Gulf region had suffered "significant production disruptions" due to the US war on Iran, they noted.
And German manufacturers have been benefitting from business being redirected to them from harder-hit parts of the global economy.
"The need for fiscal consolidation is growing," the institutes said.
The forecasts are compiled by the DIW, RWI, Ifo, IWH and IfW institutes.
The international benchmark Brent crude jumped three percent on Thursday to $106.24 per barrel.
The surge came a day after world leaders at the UN General Assembly offered little to suggest progress in ending turmoil in the oil-rich region due to the US-Israeli wars.
An adviser to Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Thursday that Tehran may expand the Middle East war to the Indian Ocean if the US or Israel attacks again.
"Since the conflict has spread from the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, it is possible that, in response to more war, the front will expand even further, reaching the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond," said Yahya Rahim Safavi in a video released by Iran's Fars news agency.
Lebanon’s National News Agency reported that Israeli artillery shelling has hit the eastern outskirts of the town of Chaqra in the Bint Jbeil district.
Earlier, Israeli forces attacked villages in the Nabatieh district in southern Lebanon, between the towns of Mayfadoun, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah and Wadi al-Salouqi, as well as the towns of Barachit and Beit Yahoun.
Moreover, the town of al-Mansouri in the Tyre district was also bombed for the second time, after previous reports of artillery shelling hours into the morning.
Indifference, the view from Gaza on the UN General Assembly
For many Palestinians in Gaza, the annual gathering of world leaders in New York at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has become increasingly disconnected from the reality they face in their war-torn territory.
As the 81st session of the UNGA enters its third day, world leaders and senior officials are discussing wars, global crises and the future of the Palestinian issue, with Gaza once again taking centre stage in speeches and diplomatic meetings.
Several countries have begun restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on Wednesday.
The measures are beginning to disrupt international routes operated by Iranian carriers, with restrictions ranging from blanket bans to the suspension of individual airlines or destinations.
Hundreds of trucks idle along the road into Iran from Turkey’s mountainous eastern border. Bustling even in normal times, the countries' largest crossing is now a make-or-break economic lifeline for Tehran as the US navy blockades its ports.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has pressed to accelerate overland trade as the blockade limits the vast majority of imports while cutting off the oil and gas sales that largely keep the economy alive.
It's the latest test of Iran's endurance. Frustrated Iranian truck drivers spoke to The Associated Press at the Turkey border crossing, where lines now stretch for miles.
“I’ve been driving through this border gate for 15 years. I’ve never had to wait as long as now,” said Muhammed Rıza Shiri, 55, who had waited four days to carry his load of rubber into Iran. “We had to wait at the end of a seven-kilometer (4.3-mile) line. We used to wait, maximum, for three days here. Because of the war, the waiting times exceed five days.”
“They are trying to create difficulties wherever they can, and they are holding nothing back. They are closing off routes, shutting down air routes, blocking land routes and trying to fuel internal divisions,” President Masoud Pezeshkian added.
Is NAZA Zionism's nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
The backlash against NAZA filmmakers shows how Israel responds when allegations of genocide made by Palestinians are echoed by members of its own society, writes Yoav Litvin.
Ten commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, up from seven a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 17, preliminary shipping data showed on Thursday.
Nine vessels entered the strait, including Supramax ships carrying metals, grain and other dry bulk cargoes, as well as an empty very large gas carrier. One Supramax carrying fertilizer exited, according to the data, as of 0423 GMT on Thursday.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their transponders turned off to avoid detection.
Before the US-Israeli war on Iran started on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large, commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels, accounting for some 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply.
Iran and the US remain far apart on how to end the war but diplomacy must continue, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday, after Iran's president told the United Nations General Assembly that Tehran would never surrender to US pressure.
The senior Iranian official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals, which prioritise lifting a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, 27 commodity vessels on Wednesday transited the waterway, up from 24 a day earlier and compared with an average of 26 ships using the strait in the past 10 days.

articles.title: A fresh $42 million, new sanctions, and a seat in the coalition rebuilding Ukraine’s Navy. Australia just signed its long-term security pact with Ukraine
articles.body:
A new bilateral security agreement puts Australia's support for Ukraine on a long-term footing, the Australian government said. The pact bundles fresh money for Kyiv, wider sanctions on Russia, and a new role for Australia in a multinational effort to rebuild Ukraine's Navy.
Australia sits half a world from the front, yet it wants what Ukraine has learned. The deal runs both ways—Australia sends money and equipment, and treats more than four years of Ukrainian war-fighting as a lesson for its own forces. One-off aid packages are giving way to long-term security pacts as Ukraine's partners lock in support—and, more and more, ask to learn from the force that has spent years fighting Russia.
A bigger package and new sanctions
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the agreement on 24 September. Albanese pledged an additional A$60 million ($42 million) in support. It splits into A$45 million ($32 million) of Australian Defence Force equipment, A$10 million for Ukraine's Energy Support Fund, and A$5 million in humanitarian aid. That lifts Australia's total contribution to almost A$1.9 billion ($1.3 billion). Australia also widened its sanctions on Russia to almost 1,900 measures and listed nearly 300 shadow-fleet vessels—the aging tankers Moscow uses to move oil around Western price caps.
“What happens in Ukraine matters in Indo-Pacific”: Australia pledged Ukraine another $70 million
Australia will also join the Maritime Capability Coalition for Ukraine, a UK- and Norway-led group building up Ukraine's Navy. The government cast the move as another two-way exchange: it helps Ukraine at sea while giving Australian planners insights into advanced maritime capabilities and their operational use.
Lessons that run both ways
The agreement frames the partnership as a trade in know-how, not just aid. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said that through deeper cooperation Australia could "lend our strengths and insights to help grow Ukraine's defence industrial base, and likewise learn from the hard-fought lessons of Ukraine's resistance in developing our future capabilities." Ukraine has shown what an innovative, agile force can do in a drone-heavy war, and Canberra wants the lessons. Australia has already supplied 49 retired M1A1 Abrams tanks and 120 Bushmaster protected vehicles, hardware Ukrainian crews took straight into frontline use. Two Australian companies are also developing Arrow interceptor drones for delivery to Ukraine.
