articles.title: Surveys Show More Americans Warming to China
articles.body:
Americans are warming to China, new surveys show.
A Pew Research Center survey published Wednesday found that the share of Americans with a cold view of China has fallen to 54% from 68% in 2021. Over the same period, the share of Americans with a warm view of China grew from 11% to 19%, while those with a neutral view grew from 20% to 27%. The findings are based on responses from 1,168 U.S. adults who were asked to rate China as part of a broader survey conducted Sept. 14-20.
Another survey published this week by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that American sentiment towards China has warmed since a record low in 2024. The survey, conducted July 10-21, showed that fewer Americans see China as a threat, with 41% considering China’s territorial ambitions a critical threat to the U.S. as compared to 52% in 2022. Americans also increasingly favor cooperation with China over containment: 57% said the U.S. should engage with China, while 40% think the U.S. should actively limit the growth of China’s power.
“There is appetite for engagement. Part of this may be recognition that better understanding is a positive,” says Ja-Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore.
Chong says the results reflect a “rebound” from pandemic-era lows of U.S. views of China. A Pew survey published in July 2020 found that 73% of Americans viewed China unfavorably—then the highest share since Pew began tracking the measure in 2005. By 2023, a separate Pew survey found that figure had risen to 83%, amid widespread concern about Beijing’s relationship with Russia and tensions over Taiwan.
Mixed politics
President Donald Trump has also signaled greater openness to Beijing, at least in its economic relationship. The “positive language coming from the White House” may have fuelled some of the shift, Chong tells TIME.
Early into his second term, Trump raised tariffs on many Chinese imports to a staggering 145% in an effort to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. His Administration also increased scrutiny of Chinese visa applicants and revoked the visas of some Chinese students, raising alarms about a “China Initiative 2.0.” The Administration also restricted sales of Nvidia’s H20 artificial intelligence chip to China and added dozens of Chinese entities to an export blacklist over national security concerns.
The Trump Administration has also continued its crackdown on “birth tourism,” a practice Trump has singled out Chinese nationals over. On Wednesday, the State Department announced that it would restrict visas for foreigners who knowingly participate in or facilitate commercial arrangements to give birth in the U.S. in order to secure their children American citizenship, a policy widely seen as an effort to restrict birthright citizenship.
But Trump has since eased some technology restrictions, pursued a trade truce, and renewed dialogue with Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday to much fanfare, marking the leaders’ third in-person meeting since Trump returned to office. Economic negotiations have been central to that diplomatic thaw, which the Chicago Council report said suggests that the Trump Administration views China primarily through an economic lens, rather than strategic competition.
“The top leadership on both U.S. and Chinese sides have made significant steps to try and arrest the downward trend in their relationship,” says Dylan Loh, associate professor of public policy and global affairs at Nanyang Technology University in Singapore. “The warming trend isn’t admiration but a moderation of threat perception, driven by a shift toward viewing China as a competitor rather than an immediate adversary as other crises take precedence.”
Still, Chong cautions: “There remains a deep reservoir of apprehension” among Americans towards China.
Trump’s MAGA Republican base remains hawkish. According to the Chicago Council survey, 63% of MAGA Republicans favor containing China rather than cooperating with it, whereas 57% of non-MAGA Republicans favor cooperation. A March 2026 poll by the Chicago Council, alongside NPR and Ipsos, found that MAGA Republicans were more likely than non-MAGA Republicans to prefer higher tariffs on Chinese imports and more restrictions on U.S.-China trade, even if it resulted in higher costs for American consumers, as well as limits on Chinese international students studying in the U.S.
Skepticism towards China is also pronounced on Capitol Hill. In a Sept. 18 letter, Rep. John Moolenaar (R, Mich.), chair of the House Select Committee on China, urged the Trump Administration to restrict Beijing’s access to U.S. AI and semiconductor technology. In December, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R, Neb.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D, Del.) also introduced legislation to block exports of advanced AI chips to China.
Lawmakers have also pressed Trump to stand firm on Taiwan as the President described a pending U.S. arms package to the island as a “negotiating chip” in talks with Beijing. Moolenaar warned against concessions on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Ricketts urged that the U.S. cannot allow China to take the island by force.
By contrast, public support for direct military intervention over Taiwan has declined. The Chicago Council study this week found that just 38% of Americans support using U.S. troops to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion, down from 52% in 2021.
Shifting global attitudes
The shift in U.S. attitudes comes as China’s global image has improved and America’s has deteriorated. A Pew survey published in July found that people in most of 36 countries surveyed viewed China more favorably than the U.S., a reversal from last year when the U.S. generally retained an advantage despite declining ratings.
Internationally, “perceptions of Washington’s unfriendly and unhelpful trade and security policies abroad and how it is causing problems to various countries' own domestic economies” has driven a shift in sentiment away from the U.S., says Loh.
The Trump Administration imposed sweeping tariffs on much of the world in April 2025, and has pursued new ones after the Supreme Court struck down the bulk of “reciprocal tariffs.” The Administration has also pulled back from international institutions and foreign aid. World leaders have also expressed concern with Trump’s expansionist rhetoric towards Canada, Greenland, Venezuela, and Cuba, as well as the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which has driven up energy prices around the world.
The U.S.-China geopolitical rivalry invites comparisons that can work in China’s favor, says Benjamin Ho, assistant professor and coordinator at the Singapore-based S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’s China Program. Disillusionment with Washington may make Beijing look more appealing by contrast, even to Americans, he adds. Domestically, Trump’s job approval rating was at a record low of 32% in September, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
“It’s easy when you’re unhappy with things at home to instead look at your peer rival,” Ho says.
Kishore Mahbubani, a Singaporean diplomat and former President of the United Nations Security Council, tells TIME that, against the backdrop of the U.S. withdrawing from the global stage, China has come across as a more dependable partner for much of the Global South.
Meanwhile, Chinese consumer brands and cultural exports have found new audiences abroad, like Pop Mart’s Labubu dolls. On TikTok, which is owned by Chinese company ByteDance outside the U.S., users have embraced Chinese customs, like drinking warm water and practicing tai chi as part of the “Chinamaxxing” trend.
Ho points to social media exposure as a significant factor in driving youth opinion. He notes that China has toned down its assertive “wolf warrior” diplomacy in favor of a more flexible approach. Many positive depictions of China online appear to be organic, although media watchdogs previously reported that Beijing has used international broadcasting and advertising campaigns to spread propaganda.
China has taken deliberate steps to project an open, positive global image, analysts say. Beijing has expanded visa-free access for foreign tourists and sought to bring in more international students. China’s foreign ministry announced in May that more than 50,000 young Americans had visited for exchanges since November 2023. Mahbubani says that as more people visit China, they “see that Chinese cities represent the future.”
China has also invested heavily in overseas infrastructure through its Belt and Road Initiative.
Young Americans were more likely to view China warmly, the Pew survey found. Americans under 50 gave China a more positive rating than those 50 and older, although younger Americans were still more likely to view China coldly.
Earlier polling also found that younger Americans are less concerned about China’s growing global power. In a 2025 survey by the Chicago Council, just 34% of Gen Z Americans view China’s power as a critical threat to the U.S., as compared to 43% of Millenials, 56% of Gen Xers, and 62% of Boomers.

articles.title: ‘No Other Choice’: Zelensky Warns Russia of Winter Strikes
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that “General Winter” could turn against Russia this year, threatening retaliatory strikes on Russian energy infrastructure if Moscow continues attacking Ukraine’s power grid and heating systems.
During his address to the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Zelensky acknowledged that the approaching winter could be extremely difficult for Ukrainians but said Russia would also face consequences.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter may be very hard for us, but in response, we will have no other choice but to make it painful for Russia as well,” Zelensky said.
“No Russian official could ever imagine that General Winter, who fought for Russia for centuries, would one day switch sides and support those defending themselves from Russia,” he added.
“We will make that happen this winter if Russia continues attacking our energy system and heating.”
The phrase “General Winter” traditionally describes the severe weather that helped Russia repel invading armies. Zelensky turned the metaphor around to warn that attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure could provoke intensified strikes against the energy resources financing Moscow’s war.
Kyiv ties retaliation to Russian attacks
Zelensky presented the warning as conditional retaliation rather than an unconditional campaign against Russian energy infrastructure.
He said Ukraine had not chosen the war and was fighting because its people had chosen “not to die.” The president called for concrete de-escalation measures before winter but argued that Kyiv could not be expected to exercise restraint while Russia continued targeting civilian utilities.
Russia Sanctions Lifted for Two Oligarchs
Zelensky also said Ukraine’s strikes were aimed not at oil, fuel, or ports for their own sake, but at Russia’s ability to finance and continue the invasion.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, storage facilities, and export infrastructure with long-range drones. Kyiv considers such facilities legitimate military targets because they supply Russian forces and generate revenue for the Kremlin’s war effort.
Proposed energy truce remains uncertain
Zelensky’s warning came one day after talks with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Previously Zelensky told Trump Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow reciprocated by ending strikes on Ukraine’s electricity, heating, and water infrastructure.
“We are ready for an energy ceasefire,” Zelensky said after the meeting. “You don’t attack these, and we will not attack these.”
Trump had announced on Sept. 14 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. However, neither side subsequently published formal terms, a list of protected sites, or a mechanism for monitoring alleged violations.
Kyiv has insisted that any pause must be reciprocal and cover every type of Russian attack against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Zelensky has also said Moscow must clearly identify which Russian facilities it wants protected and accept equivalent restrictions concerning Ukrainian electricity and gas supplies.
Another winter battle over energy
Russia has repeatedly attempted to cripple Ukraine’s electricity and heating systems during the coldest months of the war, launching waves of missiles and drones against power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has expanded its ability to strike refineries and other energy facilities deep inside Russia. The attacks have disrupted fuel production and increased the economic cost of Moscow’s invasion.
Zelensky’s UN speech suggested that Kyiv would intensify that strategy if Russia launches another winter campaign against Ukrainian utilities.
He stressed that de-escalation remained possible, but only if Moscow stopped trying to use cold weather and the destruction of civilian infrastructure as weapons.
“General Winter,” Zelensky warned, may no longer fight exclusively for Russia.

Moscow Weighs Relocating State-Owned Companies as Ukrainian Ballistic Missile Nears Flight Trials
Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development has identified eight major state-owned holding companies that may relocate parts of their operations from Moscow to regional areas.
Speaking at a meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and government members, Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov outlined the proposal, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
It follows a warning from Denys Shtilerman, chief designer at defense company Fire Point, that Ukraine could launch ballistic missile strikes against Moscow as early as this autumn.
The list prepared by the ministry includes Russian Railways, Aeroflot, Russian Post, Transneft, Rosseti, Rosneft, Inter RAO, and Zarubezhneft, according to The Moscow Times.
Reshetnikov noted that after reviewing nearly 500 state-linked companies, the ministry selected eight holdings whose corporate networks encompass approximately 250 entities and 270,000 jobs in the capital.
Reshetnikov stated that not all of these jobs are managerial. While administrative structures operate in Moscow, companies like Aeroflot, Russian Railways, and Rosseti also maintain local staff who directly provide public services.
The economic ministry framed the relocation as a measure to boost efficiency by lowering expenses, citing lower costs for salaries, rent, and office maintenance in regional areas compared to the capital.
Reshetnikov emphasized that the move would offer growth opportunities, jobs, and added tax revenue for regions, noting that several firms are already shifting accounting, IT, and legal divisions outside Moscow.
Among existing transfers, Inter RAO established HR and call center operations in the Ivanovo, Saratov, and Orel regions, while Zarubezhneft set up a corporate service center in the Samara region, The Moscow Times reported.
Russian Post moved over 1,000 IT employees to Tatarstan and plans to reallocate roughly 2,000 more. Russian Railways intends to place up to 2,000 workers in an innovation cluster in the Vladimir region, and Transneft plans to transfer about 1,000 employees out of the capital.
The invitation comes amid Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to the United States, where he met with US President Donald Trump to discuss military support and potential diplomatic pathways to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Previously, Denys Shtilerman said its FP-9 ballistic missile is one solid-fuel engine test away from flight trials, after which the company expects the weapon to begin striking targets inside Russia.
Asked when the company expects to provide the military with ballistic missiles for strikes against Russian targets, Shtilerman said the key remaining step is engine testing.

articles.title: AP compares Trump's meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin

AP compares Trump's meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin
Associated Press has compared the ceremonial welcomes US President Donald Trump gave Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian ruler Vladimir Putin.
Source: АР
Details: Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on the night of 23-24 September (Kyiv time). Trump personally met him at the foot of the aircraft steps, a gesture that is unusual, after senior officials from both countries agreed to extend their trade truce until January.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension of the truce – under which the two sides agreed to reduce tariffs and refrain from introducing new trade restrictions – in an interview with Fox News at the very moment Trump was meeting Xi at Joint Base Andrews near Washington.
AP noted that trade has become one of the main sources of tension in relations between the two superpowers, alongside issues involving artificial intelligence, Trump's conflict with Iran and China's claims over Taiwan. However, Xi Jinping's three-day visit is expected to be largely ceremonial, as evidenced by Trump's decision to meet the Chinese leader immediately after his landing rather than wait for him to arrive at the White House.
The welcoming ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, a guard of honour with different branches of the military represented and the display of the flags and the playing of the national anthems of both countries.
During the meeting, Trump sought to replicate the pomp with which he was welcomed in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to greet Trump. However, a red carpet was rolled out for Trump's Air Force One in Beijing.
The AP report noted that the long red carpet laid out for Xi Jinping's arrival was reminiscent of a similarly exceptionally long carpet that the US rolled out for Putin when he landed at a US Air Force base in Alaska last summer to attend a meeting aimed at finding ways to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
The two leaders are expected to discuss substantive issues in greater detail on 24 September, after a welcoming ceremony at the White House and a military parade. They will later exchange toasts at a formal dinner attended by technology industry leaders, including Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Elon Musk of SpaceX.
On 25 September, Xi and his wife will return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps and then visit the National Archives in Washington together. The White House said they will view historical documents highlighting the relationship between the two countries.
Background: Upon arriving in the US for his visit, Xi Jinping said that the US and China "should be partners, not rivals".

Trump vs Xi: Who holds the cards ahead of high-stakes talks?
Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington for high-stakes talks with US President Donald Trump, receiving an unusually elaborate personal welcome as the two leaders prepare to tackle disputes ranging from trade and Taiwan to Iran and artificial intelligence.
Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, rather than waiting to receive them at the White House. Taiwan is another potential flashpoint. Trump has delayed a roughly $14 billion weapons package for the island and has openly described arms sales as a negotiating tool in dealings with Beijing.
Beijing, however, has substantial leverage of its own through critical minerals and rare earths. China accounted for around 91% of global refining of magnet rare earths and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. Such materials are essential for automobiles, electronics, and sophisticated military equipment.
This dependence also intersects with Washington’s efforts to replenish weapons stocks depleted during the war with Iran. Heavy rare earths such as terbium are used in high-performance magnets found in radar systems and other military electronics, while China dominates their processing.
Iran itself could therefore become another subject of bargaining. Trump has publicly said he asked Xi not to become more deeply involved in the conflict, while Washington has also sought to limit China’s economic ties with Tehran.
Artificial intelligence rounds out another major area of competition. The US continues to control access to many of the most advanced chips, while Chinese companies have been narrowing the gap with lower-cost AI models. Ahead of the summit, Bessent said the two governments had discussed establishing a US-China AI dialogue and a mechanism for notifying each other about serious AI-related incidents.

Leader’s advisor: Iran fully prepared for defense; US aggression will bring heavy casualties
TEHRAN – A senior military advisor to Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, says Iran’s armed forces are fully prepared to defend the country in every field, warning the United States would face heavy casualties in the event of any aggression.
“In the missile, air-defense, and territorial-defense sectors, we have reached a level where, God forbid, if they (American forces) intend to land anywhere in Iran, they will certainly be destroyed,” Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, said during a televised broadcast on Tuesday.
“We have at least 10 million trained Basij personnel, who can defend all parts of the country through a distributed, mosaic-style approach and asymmetric warfare,” he said.
“People are the main pillar of the Islamic Republic’s power and national security.”
Safavi, a former chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also pointed to Iran’s significant advances in missile, drone and air-defense capabilities, as well as its monitoring of foreign military activity in the region.
“In the maritime domain, whether in the skies over the Persian Gulf or even in the Indian Ocean, we detect with our radar systems the US naval vessels currently in the region…and determine where they are located,” he said.
Safavi said Iran could carry out both defensive and retaliatory operations, adding that the outcome of a conflict would also depend on the resilience and determination of the societies involved.
“What matters is whether their social resilience in the United States is greater than Iran’s. Iran’s is certainly greater. War is a battle of wills,” Safavi said.
“Iran knows its objectives and wants to defend itself, its national interests, and its dignity.”
Safavi’s remarks come amid heightened tensions over US military activity in the region. Iran has repeatedly emphasized deterrence and territorial defense, including the role of missile and drone capabilities and the mobilization of forces across the country.
The advisor also addressed the Strait of Hormuz, saying its reopening would depend, among other things, on the lifting of the United States’ illegal naval blockade.
“The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened through US military pressure. It is Iran and Oman that can establish the mechanism for this. We are in contact with the Omanis, although public reporting indicates that the United States is preventing this,” he said.
“The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is conditional on [the US’s] accepting Iran’s terms.”
The strait connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is a major route for international energy shipments. Its security and freedom of navigation have long been central issues in relations between Iran and the United States.
Safavi said Iran’s broader objective was to establish a Persian Gulf security framework with regional states, without US involvement.
“Our objective is to permanently remove the threat to the Iranian people and, together with the countries of the region, establish lasting security and sustainable development in the Persian Gulf without the presence of the United States,” he said.

The foreign ministers of Poland and Belarus have met for the first time in a decade, as both sides indicated that they are open to thawing their long-frosty relations.
The two countries have regularly clashed in recent years, in particular over Minsk’s alliance with Moscow, the migration crisis Belarus has engineered on the Polish border, and the persecution of Belarus’s ethnic Polish minority. Warsaw, meanwhile, has supported the Belarusian democratic opposition.
However, on Tuesday this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed to reporters that he had met with his Belarusian counterpart, Maxim Ryzhenkov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Sikorski said that the initiative had come from the Belarusian side.

“When a neighbour wants to unfreeze and improve relations, Poland is the first to reach an agreement,” said Sikorski, quoted by broadcaster RMF.
“This is a first, introductory meeting, but meetings with other ministries and at other levels are also taking place,” he added, noting that Poland will also “soon be opening a new embassy building in Minsk”.
When asked what topics had been discussed, Sikorski said that they had included the border situation and regional security. Asked if he had requested that Belarus not allow Russia to fly drones and missiles through its territory, he said that this was discussed “among other things”.
The last known time that the Polish and Belarusian foreign ministers met was in October 2016, when Belarus’s Vladimir Makei visited Witold Waszczykowski in Warsaw.
Sikorski said that this week’s meeting with Ryzhenkov had been possible because the situation on their shared border – where Belarus has since 2021 encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to cross into Poland – is now “more normalised”.
Poland has installed physical and electronic barriers along the border, sent thousands of armed officers to guard it, and has banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly. Following those measures, the number of attempted crossings has fallen dramatically this year.
Sikorski also noted that relations have been improved by Belarus’s recent decisions to release political prisoners, including Polish ones. Most prominent among them is Andrzej Poczobut, a leader of the Polish community in Belarus, who had been imprisoned on trumped-up charges for five years.
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%

Minsk’s recent actions have provided “more freedom and greater reasons to try to stabilise relations”, said Sikorski. “A snowdrop can bloom if the weather is favorable.”
Belarus’s foreign ministry continued that metaphor in a post on social media on Wednesday, sharing a photo of Sikorski meeting with Ryzhenkov and writing that “snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart”.
“But we’re in it for the harvest,” added the ministry. “Let’s plant an orchard – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host.”
Last year, Belarus called for “dialogue” with Poland in order to “reduce the risk of armed clashes” amid a military build-up around the border. However, it also issued a formal protest to Poland over a demonstration in Warsaw organised by exiled opponents of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko.

News of Tuesday’s meeting was criticised by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the Polish security services under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and later as an advisor to President Andrzej Duda.
In a social media post, he said that Sikorski and media outlets are “forcibly pushing us into another reset with Belarus (and perhaps even with Russia)”. However, “Belarus chose its strategic path long ago and won’t turn away from Russia”, he added.
He asked if Poles are meant to forget about the death of Mateusz Sitek, a Polish soldier killed by a migrant from a group trying to force its way over the border from Belarus. His suspected killer, a Moroccan national, is believed by Polish prosecutors to still be in Belarus, which has refused to extradite him.
Should “we just move on as if nothing happened regarding Belarus’s involvement in the war against Ukraine and the intelligence war against Poland?” continued Żaryn.

“We believe that the authorities in Minsk cannot be trusted,” he said. “Of course, when the authorities communicate with Western partners, they promise that everything will be fine, that they want dialogue, but then their words fail to match their actions.”
“I understand that Minister Sikorski is doing everything to protect Polish interests and the sovereignty and security of his country, but I think that in Minsk they see it differently.”

articles.title: Poland scrambles military aviation for 2nd time due to fresh Russian strikes on Ukraine – Armed Forces
articles.body:
The Polish military has deployed aviation in its airspace for the second time due to Russia's fresh strikes on the territory of Ukraine, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces has reported.
During the first deployment of aviation, the Polish military reported that in connection with the strikes of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, military aviation was operating in Polish airspace. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were put on alert.
"These measures are of a preventive nature and are aimed at ensuring the safety of the airspace and protecting it, especially in areas adjacent to threatened zones," the command's message on the social network X says.
Subsequently, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported the completion of military aviation operations conducted to ensure security during Russian strikes on targets in Ukraine.
"We report that no violations of the airspace of the Republic of Poland were recorded," the command noted.
Approximately an hour after this report, the Polish military announced the repeated deployment of aviation due to fresh Russia strikes on Ukraine.
"Attention. In connection with the fresh strikes of Russia on the territory of Ukraine, carried out using air attack weapons, military aviation is operating in Polish airspace again," the report says.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces noted that in accordance with applicable procedures through the Air Operations Center – Air Component Command – the necessary forces and assets were deployed. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems went on alert again.

articles.title: Arab Centre in Washington examines shifting US Palestine policy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Arab Centre in Washington examines shifts in US policy toward Palestine and its future
The Arab Centre in Washington held its third annual conference on Palestine on Wednesday, 23 September, where experts and specialists discussed developments on the ground, shifts in US policy toward Palestine and Israel, the possibility of building on the pro-Palestinian movement in the United States, and the potential for genuine future policy changes.
The discussions are also taking place as candidates who built their election campaigns around opposition to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza have emerged. The congressional midterm elections expected in November will be a key indicator of the impact of shifts in public opinion on Congress.
Tamara Kharroub, executive director of the Arab Centre in Washington, said in her opening remarks that recent opinion polls showed that at least 55 per cent of Americans believe military aid to Israel should be stopped or reduced.
She said the net approval rating for Israel has also fallen by 67 points over the past eight years.
Kharroub noted that the midterm elections will be an important indicator of how the debate over the Palestinian issue and Palestinian rights translates into tangible electoral and political action.
This is particularly significant following the election of several progressive candidates who made Palestinian rights and opposition to military aid to Israel a central part of their campaigns.
"The support for Palestine that was once considered an electoral liability has now become part of a successful coalition," she said.
"The importance of the 2026 elections should not be measured only by the number of candidates who reach Congress but also by the emergence of political constituencies and voters for whom the Palestinian issue is a decisive factor in choosing their candidate," she added.
"Palestine has moved from being merely a foreign policy issue to being connected to civil liberties, freedom of expression, the role of money in politics, the use of US taxpayers' money, the influence of political and economic lobbying groups, international law and the issue of American democracy itself. It is a profound shift," Kharroub continued. "The balance has changed today, and the question now is, can this shift in public opinion and political activism become a fundamental change in US foreign policy?"
Lustick, Support for Israel hinders peace
Ian Lustick, a professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania, said the biggest problems and crises currently facing the Middle East are "an internal American political problem".
He said lobbying groups working on behalf of Israel control American politicians and US policy and push the United States toward war.
Speaking during a session moderated by Yousef Munir, head of the Palestine and Israel Program at the Arab Centre in Washington, Lustick said, "It must be made clear that America, particularly lobbying groups and their influence on America's policies in the region, is the main problem in the Middle East."
"Support for Israel hinders peace, fuels wars and drags America into them, diverting our attention from the threats posed by China and Russia elsewhere. Quite simply, the biggest problem in the Middle East today, or one of the biggest, is an internal American political problem," he added.
Lustick, whose latest book, "The Israel Lobby, America in the Grip of a Foreign Power", was co-written with Eli Clifton, urged people not to give up.
"The situation on the ground in Palestine is despairing and cannot be described in words. We are living through a state of frustration and horror," he remarked to TNA. "What is infuriating is the disregard of those in power for what is happening, despite the situation on the ground and what we hear about Israeli objectives aimed at emptying the land of as many Palestinians as possible through killing, repression and impoverishment."
He said his latest book is based on the premise that it is impossible to reach a two-state solution through negotiations and stressed that there "can be no expectation of any fundamental change in the situation of Palestinians living under Israeli control without ending the tight grip imposed by the Israel lobby on US policy."
"We treat Israel as if it were a crazy state, and the Israel lobby's remarkable success in ensuring there is no divergence between the positions of the United States and Israel, regardless of how extreme Israeli policies become, has strongly contributed to turning Tel Aviv into a rogue regime and an internationally isolated state," he said.
Lustick further said the Israel lobby in Washington had effects that were not anticipated in Israel, after Israeli voters became convinced that the special relationship with the United States would protect Israel from accountability regardless of the extremist policies pursued by its leaders.
"Far-right politicians have outperformed their moderate rivals by exploiting the fears of the Israeli population and convincing them that American support for Israel is firmly entrenched and unwavering. Thus, Israel today is the product of the success achieved by the Israel lobby in the United States," the write said.
Lustick stressed that defeating and sidelining the Israel lobby in the United States is an urgent necessity because of the danger it poses to the country.
"Our book reveals how the Israel lobby represents not only a threat to American national interests abroad but also to American freedoms at home," he added.
He called for a one-state solution in which the real struggle would be for equality, rather than the current situation, considering it the option currently available and saying its consequences would emerge within one or two generations.
He stressed that the fundamental reason behind smear campaigns waged by lobbying groups and Israel supporters against its critics, accusing them of being "jihadists, terrorists, communists and antisemites", is their inability to convince Americans of Israeli policies funded by taxpayers' money.
"It has become extremely exhausting and difficult to challenge the narrative that America has no choice but to support Israel," he added.
Lustick described the two-state solution as a "safe political option" used by most Democrats and Republicans, considering it "impossible to achieve", arguing that the main motivation behind it is to avoid raising the issue of Palestinian democratic rights amid their complete, undisclosed subordination to Israeli lobbying groups.
"We should not abandon the struggle to end the occupation. The occupation must end, but it will not end through regional agreements or military withdrawals. It will end through democratic transformation," he said.
Abu Salem, destruction has not stopped
In the second session, titled "Assessing the Situation on the Ground", moderated by Georgetown University anthropology professor Laurie King, Jihad Abu Salem, executive director of the Gaza Genocide Centre, said the current situation, nearly a year after the ceasefire, was transforming Palestinian suffering from an emergency into a permanent and painful reality.
"The killing has not stopped. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began," he said. "This does not represent the end of a war, but merely a reduction in intensity, and the destruction has not stopped. Nearly 11,000 buildings have been destroyed during this period, raising the proportion of damaged buildings in Gaza to more than 82 per cent. Most of the population are living in tents, among damaged buildings or in temporary shelters."
He added, "The committee tasked with rebuilding Gaza is drawing up plans for a territory whose residents are treated as nothing more than an obstacle to a real estate project."
Yara Asi, an assistant professor at the University of Central Florida's College of Global Health and Management, addressed the increasing targeting of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank in recent years.
She said the period from January to mid-September this year saw more than 1,600 settler attacks on Palestinians, an average of six attacks a day, according to figures from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
Omar Rahman, a researcher at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said, "Agreements such as Oslo with Israel placed the Palestinian leadership, which acts as a security partner with Israel, under military occupation and control and hostage to Western funding."
"This led to the separation of the Palestine Liberation Organisation from Palestinian communities in the diaspora, which once formed the backbone of the national movement. The bureaucratic requirements of the Palestinian Authority, such as paying salaries, maintaining security coordination and ensuring continued support from donors, also became prioritised over the PLO's priorities and the struggle for Palestinian rights," he added.
Fourth session
In the fourth session, moderated by journalist Sarah Yassin, historian specialising in the modern Middle East Asal Rad, author of the recently published book "This Is Not a Book About Palestine, How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide", discussed the anti-Palestinian bias in the US media narrative.
"Many people ask me, as someone of Iranian origin, why I am obsessed with Palestine. For me, this issue is the lens through which we understand people," Rad said. "Because if you read the real history, you will be stunned that it was allowed to happen and that it is still happening in Palestine. This is why people are angry, because the story they were told is completely different from the truth. There are literally attempts to erase this group of people. To cancel the existence of Palestinians. The Zionist argument of a land without a people for a people without a land ignores the reality of a people subjected to forced expulsion, massacres and killing, which explains our current situation."
She added, "What is the purpose of establishing the United Nations?" The aim was to establish international law and stop wars, prevent encroachment on the borders of others, guarantee sovereignty and ensure the right to self-determination of indigenous peoples. These were its core aims and tasks. Yet the establishment of Israel in historic Palestine, and the massacres and displacement of Palestinians that accompanied it, completely contradict all those principles."
She stressed that she believes that unless this wrongdoing is addressed and the situation corrected, the world will continue to live under a false international system characterised by contradiction and double standards.
The final session raised questions about possible changes. It was moderated by Ryan Grim, founder of Drop Site.
The session included Corey Archibald, co-founder of AIPAC Tracker, which tracks those who receive money from the Israel lobby, particularly the American Israel Public Affairs Committee; Lara Friedman, president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace; Daniel Levy, president of the US/Middle East Project; Josh Ruebner, policy director at the Institute for Middle East Understanding; and Shibley Telhami, Anwar Sadat Professor for Peace and Development at the University of Maryland.
The participants put forward several proposals and plans for action.
These included continuing to make Palestinian rights a priority so that politicians cannot ignore them, linking them to American values such as human rights, justice and freedom of expression, highlighting the negative economic effects and the impact of spending money on foreign wars and supporting Israel on domestic politics, and focusing on the consequences for those who ignore the shift in public opinion.
They also called for continuing efforts to pass legislation in Congress, such as halting the shipment of bombs to Israel even if the chances of passage are slim.
The aim would be to build a bloc that sends messages to future congressional leadership and the next administration while defending the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) and maintaining the legitimacy of the refugee issue as a core issue.
Daniel Levy stressed the need to make greater use of the settlements issue in a way that would force Israel to change its conduct or reconsider some matters.
"Clearly, we have a very long way to go, but we see policy proposals on the table, and the settlements issue can be used to begin this process," he said. "Raising fundamental questions such as who finances them, who provides the mortgages and who invests in them draws attention to the fact that there are no independent settlement entities, as Israeli banks and institutions are involved. We have a thread that can be followed to uncover the facts."
He also called for moving beyond the framework of the two-state solution, considering that it allows politicians to say they support a two-state solution without taking any action.
The participants stressed the need to normalise the idea of imposing sanctions on Israel and banning arms sales to it.
They also called for focusing on the 2028 presidential election and supporting a candidate who backs ending arms supplies to Israel.
They called for making use of the shift in public opinion by increasing efforts over the next two years to achieve a real transformation that would lead to ending US support for Israel's war of genocide and ending apartheid.
They also called for turning the current momentum into permanent organising that would lead to a new normal in which Israel is condemned.
They stressed the need not to accept the equation that the departure of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would mean the end of the occupation problem.
The Arab Centre distributed to attendees and participants a book titled "The Israeli Genocide in Gaza", edited by Khalil Dahshan and Tamara Kharroub.
In remarks to The New Arab, Kharroub said the recently published book by the Arab Centre addresses a range of issues related to genocide amid attempts by Israel and its allies to whitewash Israeli crimes.
"We have also seen attempts to destroy material evidence of the genocide, so we collected chapters written by prominent experts and academics in various Middle East studies and experts on Palestinian affairs to document the genocide and record the crimes committed by Israel in Gaza. We also wanted to document how the international system, through its political and legal structures and corporations, enabled and facilitated this genocide," she said.

articles.title: Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
articles.body:
Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
After a long pause, Russia’s authorities have renewed their campaign of nationalizing assets held by foreign companies — and they’ve gone big. On Thursday, Vladimir Putin issued a decree putting assets worth €6 billion under external management — specifically, the Russian divisions of retail chains Auchan and Leroy Merlin, food manufacturer Nestle and FM Logistics. Putin appointed an obscure company to manage them, with a former police general as its figurehead.
- Officially, the measure is not nationalization. Putin has imposed external management on the companies, not legally transferred their assets. This scheme was devised in 2023 and formed the basis by which Russia’s authorities seized hundreds of assets from Western owners — from energy firms to brewers and dairy companies. Foreign shareholders retain technical ownership but are stripped of all management rights (the right to repatriate profits was removed in 2022).
- Once a Russian asset is placed under external management, Western shareholders are often forced to sell to a Kremlin-backed owner, as in the case of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg. To complete the deals, Putin then suspends his own decree. But this is not always the case. Dozens of subsidiaries of Western companies have remained under external management for years.
- By default, Rosimushchestvo (the Federal Agency for State Property Management) takes charge of any assets that are put under local management by a presidential decree. But that route can be overruled. Often, assets are immediately acquired by a third party with the Kremlin's blessing. That is what is happening here. The Russian operations of Auchan, Nestle and FM Logistics went to a special purpose vehicle called LEV Management, a ready-made legal entity purchased by unknown individuals just before Putin issued his decree. The CEO is an obvious figurehead: Police Major General Andrei Krayushkin, who worked as deputy head of the Interior Ministry’s migration department in the late 2010s. Nobody has yet uncovered who is behind him.
- The Kremlin often justifies asset seizure on political grounds. For example, in 2023 many linked the decision to place Denmark’s Carlsberg under external management to Copenhagen’s willingness to supply F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine. Moscow views EU countries — and those in the “coalition of the willing” in particular — as its main opponents. With the exception of Switzerland’s Nestle, most of the affected companies are French. But why France has been singled out is unclear. Right now the Kremlin is in a bigger conflict with Germany, yet Metro Group, a German rival to Auchan, works without problem in Russia.
- Beyond politics, there are economic issues at play. First, amid fresh reports of a budget shortfall in Ukraine, plans to confiscate €200 billion of Russian reserves frozen in Europe since 2022 are back under discussion. This is a highly sensitive issue in Moscow, and all Russia has to threaten in return is the confiscation of foreign assets and funds already frozen in Russia. In this context, placing French companies with assets worth at least 600 million rubles (€6 billion) under external management looks like an attempt to gain a bargaining chip in the event of a future war of asset freezes.
- The Russian government’s own dire need for funds should not be overlooked. Over the first eight months of 2026, the budget deficit has already reached 2.5% of GDP. Placing a company under external management is not the same as nationalization. Russia does not have the right to sell Auchan and FM Logistics, nor plunder funds from their accounts to finance, for example, military expenses. But if Western countries move to confiscate Russian assets, this is the most likely next step.
Why the world should care
For whatever reason, the Russian government is reopening its battle with Western companies, in the biggest cases of de facto nationalization since 2024.

articles.title: Suspected Russian drones crash in Romania, Moldova
articles.body:
Suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight on Sept. 24, amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.
Moldovan police said in a post on Facebook that a drone with "specific elements of the 'Gerbera' type used by the Russian Federation" was found in the country's Floresti district.
Another drone violated Romania's airspace for around four minutes before crashing near Solca, Suceava County, Digi24 reported.
Romania did not blame Russia directly but acting Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruța told the outlet that a protest to Moscow over the incident was required.
No casualties were reported in either country.
The incidents came amid a prolonged drone and missile attack on Ukraine, with Chernivtsi Oblast Governor Ruslan Osypenko saying Russian drones were targeting "border infrastructure, specifically international border crossing points on the Ukrainian-Romanian and Ukrainian-Moldovan borders."
Russian drones and missiles have routinely violated the airspace of both Romania and Moldova in recent months.
A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone that violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on Sept. 8 nearly hit President Volodymyr Zelensky's plane as it was departing from Moldova.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed, the fourth such instance of a suspected Russian drone incursion this year.
A day later on Aug. 17, a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa, before crashing in a cornfield approximately 3 kilometers (1.8 miles) outside of the village of Talmaz, in the Stefan Voda district of Moldova.

articles.title: Sybiha calls for stronger sanctions pressure on Russia, more air defense systems amid attacks on Ukrainian data centers
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Russia is currently focusing its efforts on strikes against Ukrainian data centers, critical civilian infrastructure, and called for stronger sanctions pressure and more air defense systems.
“Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid warnings about missile and drone threats are crucial – they save lives,” he said in a post on X on Wednesday.
Sybiha stressed that “this is critical civilian infrastructure that provides people with access to life-saving information. It is not a military target. It is necessary for the normal functioning of everyday life.”
“As Russia fails to achieve its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians. Increasing sanctions pressure and the number of air defense systems is the only way to stop this terror. These attacks must not become the new normal,” Sybiha said.
The minister said that while the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is focused on peace efforts and diplomatic measures to end the war, Ukraine is again facing powerful Russian attacks. Two people were killed and more than 40 injured in the Russian strikes, which continued throughout the night and morning, he said. A university building in Kyiv was also hit while students were on campus.

articles.title: Trump gives Xi rare airport welcome as Chinese leader begins US state visit
articles.body:
Trump gives Xi rare airport welcome as Chinese leader begins US state visit
US President Donald Trump personally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping at a military airfield outside Washington on Wednesday, kicking off a lavish state visit focused on trade, artificial intelligence and Iran, as the two powers seek to preserve a fragile diplomatic and economic truce.
US President Donald Trump treated Chinese President Xi Jinping to a rare personal airport welcome Wednesday, kicking off a pomp-filled state visit aimed at smoothing superpower tensions on everything from AI and trade to Iran.
The summit is expected to be more about spectacle than substance – but there was an early breakthrough when Washington announced a two-month extension of a trade truce with Beijing that was due to expire in November.
After officials literally rolled out the red carpet, Trump and First Lady Melania shook hands with Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan once the Chinese president descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.
Trump, wearing a long coat and gloves, and Xi then stood side by side on the tarmac as a military band played national anthems.
A noisy flyover by two B-1 bombers clearly jolted the 80-year-old Trump, who grimaced at the roar of jets, while his Chinese guest stood by impassively.
Trump brushed off the fact that Xi had not given him a similar airport welcome when he visited Beijing in May.
"I thought it was a great little meeting, a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it," Trump told reporters at the White House after welcoming Xi.
Iran, AI, trade
The lavish visit – the third between Xi and Trump since the US leader returned to power – will include a formal welcome and another flyover, talks in the Oval Office and a state banquet at the White House on Thursday.
It will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.
Expectations of any breakthroughs are low. Analysts say the main aim of the pageantry is to maintain a fragile calm between the superpower rivals.
The Iran war will be on the agenda, Trump confirmed Wednesday, despite having earlier played down reports that Beijing was supplying Tehran with intelligence as the conflict drags on.
"I'll be talking about that and many other subjects – but it's all coming along well, including that," Trump said when an AFP reporter asked if he would bring up Iran.
On the simmering trade war sparked by Trump's sweeping tariffs last year, US Treasury Scott Bessent announced Wednesday after intensive pre-summit talks that there had been an extension of a truce.
The "economic detente" will now extend beyond its November 10 deadline to January 10, Bessent said.
But hopes of business deals have been dimmed by the fact that there are no Chinese CEOs in Xi's delegation, two sources told AFP.
In contrast, top US tech bosses including the leaders of major AI companies are set to attend Thursday's banquet.
'Oppressive dictator'
AI is set to dominate the summit amid growing fears – boosted by warnings from AI CEOs – that the technology risks wiping out humanity.
China and the United States are racing for supremacy in the field, viewing it as crucial for the rest of the century.
Preliminary talks on Sunday between Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included discussion of creating a communication channel for AI concerns.
But overall the idea is to extend the "gentleman's agreement" to reduce tensions between Beijing and Washington despite their rivalry, Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP.
Trump's five-star welcome for Xi has drawn criticism from China hawks within his own party, especially amid reports that Beijing supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.
"Our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator," said Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the powerful Senate Armed Services Committee.
But for Trump, Xi's visit is also a chance to focus on pageantry instead of problems at home, where the Iran war's effect on fuel prices has sent his approval rating plummeting to historic lows ahead of midterm elections in November.
The last American president to welcome a foreign leader at Andrews – except for papal visits – was John F. Kennedy in 1962, although Trump welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin off his plane in Alaska last year.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts
Ukrainian forces struck a drone warehouse belonging to Russia’s Rubicon unmanned systems unit in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region, along with several UAV command posts and logistics facilities, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 23, the strikes were carried out on September 22 and overnight into September 23 against Russian military facilities across the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Ukrainian forces targeted Russian UAV command posts near Novoselivka Persha and Dachne in the Donetsk region. A separate strike hit a drone warehouse operated by the Rubicon unit near Volnovakha, according to the General Staff.
The operation also targeted Russian military logistics. A fuel and lubricants depot was struck near Kundriuche in the Luhansk region, while logistics warehouses were hit near Hirnyk and Velyka Shyshivka in the Donetsk region.
Near Krasnohorivka, Ukrainian forces also struck a concentration of personnel belonging to a Russian UAV unit, the General Staff said. The extent of the damage at the sites was not immediately disclosed.
Rubicon, formally known as Russia’s Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies, was established in August 2024 under the Russian Defense Ministry to centralize the development, testing, training, and battlefield deployment of unmanned systems. The unit operates FPV and fixed-wing drones and also maintains dedicated electronic warfare and counter-drone capabilities.
According to a June 2026 analysis by the Foreign Policy Research Institute, Rubicon expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to around 5,000 by spring 2026. Its combat detachments have been used to target Ukrainian drone crews and logistics networks behind the front line while testing new equipment and tactics for wider use by Russian forces.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian attack drone storage and launch site in the Oryol region, damaging five launchers and at least three storage facilities, according to Ukraine’s General Staff. The facility was reportedly used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones against Ukraine.

Ukrainian artillery troops strike Russian equipment and positions in Huliaipole – video
Ukrainian soldiers from the 7th Air Assault Corps, together with the 44th Separate Artillery Brigade named after Hetman Danylo Apostol, have struck Russian artillery systems, armoured vehicles and personnel in Huliaipole, Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
Source: 7th Air Assault Corps
Details: The military said the Russians view Huliaipole as a foothold for further offensive operations towards Zaporizhzhia.
The 7th Air Assault Corps noted that the city's built-up areas allow Russian forces to secretly accumulate personnel and equipment, deploy command posts and artillery positions, and establish drone launch sites.

Quote: "Artillery troops struck enemy personnel, self-propelled guns, howitzers, other artillery systems and armoured vehicles. Some of the targets were detected directly at firing positions.
Among the destroyed equipment was a T-55 tank. It is a medium tank designed for operations in conditions involving the use of nuclear weapons and was adopted by the Soviet Army in the 1950s."

articles.title: Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM
articles.body:
Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM
Russian crude supplies helped cushion India from an oil-supply shock after the conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, showing Moscow’s reliability as an energy partner, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said. 
Rudenko’s statement comes amid renewed scrutiny on India’s Russian oil purchases, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law. 
Indian refiners turned heavily to Russian crude after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to handle roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies. 
The scale of the shift was most visible in March, when India’s Russian crude imports nearly doubled from the previous month to 2.25 million barrels per day (bpd) and accounted for half of its oil purchases. 
Gulf shipments to India simultaneously plunged 61% to 1.18 million bpd. Existing arrangements between Moscow and New Delhi helped “significantly mitigate” the consequences of disruptions to global energy trade, Rudenko told Russian news outlet NEWS.ru on Wednesday.
It showed Moscow could meet demand from its partners even in difficult geopolitical conditions, he added.
Good to meet @SecRubio of the US #UNHighLevelWeek
Reiterated India’s interests and concerns with regard to SRIA. Also discussed the Gulf and Ukraine situations.
🇮🇳 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/163YRVlMZG
Meanwhile, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar, who is in New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly meeting, raised New Delhi’s concerns about the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday. 
The law gives US President Donald Trump the authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top buyers of Russian oil and gas. India’s Russian oil purchases have eased from record summer levels as other supplies recovered, but Moscow remains India’s largest crude supplier.
Russian shipments stood at about 2.1 million bpd in August, and are tracking at around 1.9 million bpd in September, according to preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler. India has maintained that securing affordable and dependable energy for its 1.4 billion people requires multiple suppliers, and warned against restrictions that could distort or constrict global energy markets.
Russia’s energy cooperation with India extends beyond oil. Rudenko pointed to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in southern India built in collaboration with Russia and said another site will soon be allocated for a Russian-designed nuclear facility.

articles.title: Latvian defence technology companies seek US partners for joint development and manufacturing
articles.body:
Latvian defence and dual-use technology companies are meeting with US industry firms Neros, Anduril, Shield AI, Kratos Defense & Security Solutions, Qualcomm and Starling Systems in Los Angeles and San Diego. The programme, organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), is taking place during Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs’ working visit to the United States. It aims to help Latvian developers and manufacturers find US customers, investors, systems integrators and manufacturing partners, and explore opportunities to participate in joint product development, testing and supply chains.
“The United States is one of the world’s largest defence technology markets. It is home to global systems integrators and investors capable of funding rapid product development and the scaling of manufacturing. Latvia’s exports of goods and services to the US exceeded €1 billion in 2025, and our next ambition is to increase the share of high-value technology in those exports. Latvian companies are bringing their own solutions, engineering expertise and manufacturing capabilities to these discussions. The goal is to find partners with whom they can jointly develop, test and manufacture new products. The value of these talks will be measured by the technical cooperation, orders and investment that follow,” says Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Economics.
Southern California: Talks with Next-Generation Defence Technology Companies
The Latvian delegation will meet Neros, Anduril, Shield AI, Kratos Defense & Security Solutions, Qualcomm and Starling Systems in Los Angeles and San Diego. Discussions will cover potential cooperation in component supply, joint product development, testing and manufacturing, as well as opportunities for Latvian companies to join their US partners’ supply chains. Each Latvian company is participating in meetings relevant to its specialisation and commercial objectives.
A business roundtable is also planned in Torrance, where the Latvian delegation will meet defence and dual-use technology companies from the surrounding area. The discussion will focus on the technologies Latvian companies can offer, joint product development and manufacturing, and opportunities to participate in US supply chains.
Collectively, these US companies work in fields that include tactical and autonomous unmanned systems, counter-drone solutions, defence electronics, AI-based control software, sensors, radio communications, semiconductors, connectivity and high-performance computing, as well as space, hypersonic and rocket propulsion technologies.
Technologies in these fields are used for reconnaissance, target identification, carrying various payloads, protecting facilities and military units, processing and transmitting data, and operating autonomously when communications or navigation signals are disrupted or unavailable. Such systems require secure data transmission, radio electronics, sensors, energy-efficient semiconductors, software and the integration of different technologies into a single system.
Latvian companies can offer electronics and communications modules, sensors, software, systems integration expertise and manufacturing capabilities in these areas. The meetings are intended to establish which Latvian solutions meet US partners’ technical requirements and where Latvian companies could contribute to technology development, testing, manufacturing or supply chains. Practical cooperation will depend on an assessment of technical requirements, compatibility and commercial terms.
“Latvian companies combine strong engineering expertise with the ability to develop and adapt technologies quickly to real defence needs. We see potential for cooperation in unmanned systems, secure communications, sensors, software and systems integration. Working with Latvian partners could help develop and test solutions that strengthen allied technological readiness and interoperability on NATO’s eastern flank. During this visit, we want to identify specific joint projects and agree on the next steps in technical cooperation,” says Ido Gur, founder and CEO of Starling Systems.
San Diego: Autonomy, Military Aviation and Connectivity
San Diego is one of the leading US centres for military aviation, unmanned systems and defence technology. Separate meetings with US partners are planned there, taking into account the capabilities and development goals of the Latvian companies involved.
Discussions will focus on autonomous platforms operating in complex electromagnetic environments, secure data transmission, sensors, the use of artificial intelligence, interoperability between systems and the integration of different technologies into a single product. Connectivity, semiconductors and on-device data processing needed for energy-efficient autonomous systems will also be discussed.
Latvian companies’ experience in electronics, secure data transmission, sensors, software and systems integration provides a basis for technical discussions with US partners. The meetings will explore whether specific Latvian products or engineering capabilities could contribute to joint projects or supply chains. Another possible area of discussion is adapting technologies to the requirements of European allies, where both sides see a technical and commercial case for doing so.
Latvia Offers Technology, Engineers and Manufacturing Expertise
The defence and dual-use technology programme includes Aumeux, SAF North America, Origin Robotics, Raw-tech, Ardlat, Perkons Energy, LMT, LMT Defence and VIC TEC. It also includes the Latgale Special Economic Zone, the Latvian Exporters’ Association “The Red Jackets”, the Latvian Federation of Security and Defence Industries, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the University of Latvia and Riga Technical University.
“The Latvian delegation’s offering is not limited to one product or technology. It brings together expertise in unmanned and counter-drone systems, radio communications, electronics, sensors, software, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and manufacturing. Our task is to find a place for these technologies in specific projects run by US companies. The mission’s results will be determined not by the number of meetings, but by the companies’ ability to continue technical discussions after the visit, move towards testing and establish commercially viable partnerships,” says Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.
One example of Latvia’s technology offering is SAF Tehnika, which develops and manufactures microwave radio equipment for high-capacity data transmission, solutions for ultra-low-latency networks and portable radio-frequency spectrum analysers in Riga. This equipment is used to test communications quality, analyse radio signals and detect interference.
“The US is the world’s wealthiest market, and every exporter dreams of securing a place at the table. LIAA has done tremendous work in arranging meetings with some of the most important US companies in the dual-use sector. A small, motivated LIAA team has achieved what larger countries do with many times the resources. I have been eagerly awaiting my arrival in California to take part in this valuable programme,” says Jānis Bergs, Member of the Management Board and Vice President of Sales and Business Development at SAF Tehnika.
After the visit, Latvian companies will continue discussions with partners where specific technical or commercial opportunities have been identified. LIAA will support the coordination of contacts, provide guidance on the US market and help identify suitable export and investment support instruments.
The defence and dual-use technology programme is part of LIAA’s Latvian business trade mission to the United States, which runs until 27 September and covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. Separate programmes have also been prepared for startups, film industry companies and life sciences companies.
LIAA organises participation in international trade missions under the EU-co-financed Innovative Business Development Programme for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs), with support from the European Regional Development Fund and national funding. Companies may participate either by paying their own costs or by receiving support to cover eligible expenses.

articles.title: Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.
articles.body:
Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.
Construction of a new Bocharov Ruchey residence for Vladimir Putin is nearing completion in Sochi: the old buildings there were demolished in 2024, and by the fall of 2026 new ones had already gone up in their place. The general contractor for the construction is the Crimea-based Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, which is tied to Putin’s friend Arkady Rotenberg, BBC Russia reports.
A classified state defense contract for the FSO covers the reconstruction of the Bocharov Ruchey residence, but journalists found the contract’s 25-digit identifier in court records. The digits show the contract covers 2023–2027, that it was awarded without competitive bidding or an auction, and that its price was fixed.
The general contractor is the Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, whose beneficiary is believed to be developer Alexei Fomenko. Russian media have linked Fomenko to Arkady Rotenberg. The company also built dachas in occupied Crimea for Vladimir Putin and Alexander Bortnikov, director of Russia’s Federal Security Service, and carried out the reconstruction of the Artek children’s camp.
BBC could not determine the total cost of the contract to reconstruct Bocharov Ruchey, but the scale can be gauged from publicly available job postings for individual construction subcontracts. Those postings listed work budgets of 90, 150, 250, 400, and 500 million rubles.
Workers for the construction site were recruited through social media and job-listing websites. The postings described the site as a “strategic facility” and warned candidates that they would face strict background checks. Builders were promised piece-rate pay in cash, three meals a day, and accommodation in a “hostel with a pool.”
BBC says construction at Bocharov Ruchey has continued even though Putin has visited Sochi far less often since Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine began. According to calculations by the Financial Times, he visited there 24 times before the full-scale war, 13 times in 2022, and only twice a year in both 2024 and 2025, as Ukrainian drones increasingly reached the Black Sea coast.
