articles.title: America, China and the Evolving New World Order
articles.body:
On Thursday, President Xi Jinping of China is meeting President Donald Trump at the White House. The United States and China are in significantly different places and the world increasingly fragmented and multi-polar since he last visited the White House to meet President Barack Obama in 2015. As the American and Chinese leaders meet, the most consequential question is: who is shaping the international order, and according to whose principles and rules?
The answer may be more nuanced than many expected: while the U.S. remains the world’s most powerful country, China is emerging as an architect of that order.
Beijing is creating institutions, proposing diplomatic initiatives, establishing technological standards and offering infrastructure to countries across the world. But its influence extends beyond diplomacy. China offers developing countries alternative paths to prosperity, mobilizing its technological champions as sources of power. Rather than replicating the American system of military alliance and security guarantees, Beijing is building networks of trade and alternative financial institutions. China is also promoting a new vocabulary of international affairs—one that is deliberately distinct from the American language of power.
China does not have a miraculous, surefire plan to succeed the U.S. as the world’s new hegemon. Nor is there evidence that other countries are prepared to embrace a Chinese-led system entirely. China’s ambition appears more complicated: it seeks greater influence over the ideas and institutions that determine how the international system works. Beijing wants not merely a decisive vote in the game, but a hand in writing its rules.
Beijing is pursuing this ambition at a moment when Washington, despite its power, appears less willing to shoulder the traditional burdens of global leadership. Its domestic political divisions, the Trump Administration’s apparent disregard for international law, and its erratic approach to foreign policy and global conflicts have raised questions about the future of American stewardship.
Yet China is not inheriting a vacuum. Thanks to its power, Washington remains deeply entrenched in the institutions, alliances, and technologies that underpin its supremacy. China is gaining room to shape the international order, but it is not yet replacing the power that built much of it. Instead, Beijing is creating alternatives that allow other countries to become less dependent on the existing American-led system.
China’s new new world vision
Perhaps the most powerful element of China’s vision for a different international order is not its defense of national sovereignty or multipolarity, but its proposition about development. Beijing is asking a pointed question: what if countries need not follow the Western path to modernity?
For much of the past eight decades, the prevailing vision of development was associated with a broadly Western model: foreign aid, privatization, and political liberalization. China offers something different, defying the hopes of Western intellectuals and policymakers who believed that Beijing’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 would eventually lead to its political liberalization.
China’s own experience suggests that economic success can be built, at least partly, through investments in infrastructure, financed by public finance and state loans. The old Chinese expression about “getting richer by building roads” has also shaped its approach abroad: Beijing has committed itself to financing and promoting across the Global South the type of infrastructure that helped power its own economic miracle.
The developing world has been receptive. China’s Global Development Initiative places development at the center of its international engagement. Although the Belt and Road Initiative has been heavily criticized since its inception, it has provided Beijing with a practical platform for financing and building infrastructure overseas. Beijing is making its case not through elegantly written standards of governance but through tangible things: roads, railways, and ports.
Over the past decade, the Chinese government and its state-owned enterprises invested approximately $634 billion into building physical infrastructure around the world, along with $419 billion in direct investments outside the financial sector in the developing world. For many governments in Latin America—a region Washington has long regarded as its strategic backyard—access to Chinese development finance and Chinese markets has led to significant economic gains.
China’s development strategy creates economic relationships that should endure for decades, especially when its financing carries conditions that serve Beijing’s interests, including privileged access to critical minerals and resources. But the era of immense Chinese overseas spending is becoming harder to sustain as Beijing grapples with its own economic woes.
The ultimate test of Beijing’s economic statecraft, then, is whether it can build lasting relationships across the globe that rest on more than financial largesse and accumulated diplomatic capital. China must demonstrate that it understands what developing countries actually need and that those needs will evolve over time.
A new age of Chinese tech
Influence is no longer exerted through explicit military might but built quietly into the infrastructure of everyday economic life. As development becomes increasingly intertwined with technology, a country that adopts Chinese cloud computing may also embed itself in a Chinese-led ecosystem that endures for decades.
Artificial intelligence offers the clearest example of technology as a source of geopolitical power. China is rapidly promoting its AI capabilities globally, including open-weight models that can be deployed at a fraction of the cost of their Western competitors. For much of the developing world, the appeal is obvious: those countries can gain access to cutting-edge technology without having to rely exclusively on American tech giants.
The technological race is also becoming a competition over the development choices countries make. If most economies build their digital infrastructure and AI systems primarily around American technologies, Washington will retain an enormous structural advantage. As countries invest in those systems, they will become increasingly dependent on them, while American tech giants gain access to vast stores of user data. If more countries come to rely on Chinese technologies and the standards and supply chains associated with them, China will acquire greater influence: less visible than military power, but potentially just as consequential and enduring.
This is why China’s enormous industrial capacity has become a central instrument of its effort to shape the global order. Beijing is not merely exporting products: it is helping determine which technologies countries use to modernize themselves, and by extension, the systems their economies will rely on.
A central ambiguity lies at the heart of China’s development strategy. Chinese technology can expand a country’s economic opportunities but is bound to increase its dependence on China. That tension is likely to persist longer than many anticipated. Many governments are choosing Chinese technology for its affordability and not because they have been persuaded by Beijing’s governing philosophy. A country may adopt Chinese systems while remaining aligned with the U.S. on security.
China therefore does not depend on others becoming “pro-China”. It may be enough for them to become less dependent on the West. This is a vital distinction. Beijing need not convince the world that its model is superior. It only needs to show that alternatives to Western technologies exist. The cumulative effect of those alternatives could gradually alter the balance of the global order.
China’s statecraft is a way of redistributing economic and technological power. Unlike the U.S., China’s most significant export may not be a political model but the infrastructure and technology through which other countries seek to build prosperity. In adopting those systems, they become part of a world less dominated by the U.S. and its European allies.
Networks, not alliances
Before arriving in Washington, President Xi undertook a flurry of overseas travel, visiting places that American presidents have largely neglected: Bishkek, Cairo, New Delhi. His itinerary illuminated an interesting pattern. Each of his September stops connected China to the expanding international networks Beijing has championed and some Western governments regard with suspicion, notably the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and BRICS.
Consider BRICS. What began as an informal gathering of emerging economies has become a much larger political forum, with countries from the Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere seeking membership or closer connections. It would be a mistake to consider BRICS as a Beijing-led anti-American bloc. Its members have sharply different interests, and countries such as India have no intention of joining an anti-Western alliance. But the group’s expansion reflects a critical shift: a growing number of countries want access to institutions in which the Group of 7 does not set the terms.
The Group of 7 is an exclusive club whose members broadly share political values and standards of governance. China does not demand that other countries abandon institutions led by Washington; instead, it builds alternatives that exist alongside them. That distinction matters.
This is why I expect that the emerging world order will not be divided neatly between a Chinese camp and an American one. Most countries will continue to use the dollar, trade with the U.S., and participate in Western institutions while simultaneously joining BRICS, borrowing from Chinese-backed institutions, and engaging with the SCO. For many governments, the fundamental attraction is the freedom to choose among competing sources of finance, technology, and diplomatic support.
Beijing’s advocacy of multipolarity is neither merely about building a fairer world, nor is it about replacing one hegemon with another. It is an attempt to widen the range of choices available to other states. By establishing new institutions and initiatives, Beijing is accelerating the movement of power away from the traditional centers of the West. For China, being an architect of the international order does not necessarily mean replacing America, but building a world where the U.S. can no longer design all the rules or define legitimate international behavior by itself.
Yet the China dilemma remains. Beijing opposes an international order dominated by a single power, but fragmenting that system would inevitably increase China’s global influence. And the more influence China acquires, the more other countries may begin to question whether Beijing’s vision is truly intended to produce greater equality, or merely a new distribution of power that benefits China most.
An order shaper in the making
President Xi’s meeting with President Trump will be scrutinized for the usual signs of rivalry: tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic tensions. But beneath those headlines lies the great contest over how the international order itself should work.
China is not seeking to inherit the world America built. It is trying to change how that world works by giving other countries choices beyond the American-led system. For decades, the U.S. was identified with policing the rules-based international order, while China was portrayed primarily as its challenger. But during President Trump's second term, questions of sovereignty and international law have themselves become more contested, blurring what once seemed a clear distinction between the American and Chinese approaches.
Whether China’s ascent produces a fairer international order, a more genuinely multipolar one, or simply a new system in which Chinese power carries greater weight remains uncertain. The answer will depend not only on what Beijing wants, but also on what other countries are willing to accept. For now, China’s ambition may not be to write all the rules, but to ensure that Washington is no longer the only power capable of writing them.

articles.title: Russia’s Global Recruitment Pipeline: How Russia Hunts the World’s Poor to Feed Its War in Ukraine – Part 2
articles.body:
You can find Part 1 here.
If Africa is one front in this campaign, South Asia is arguably the largest.
CNN has reported estimates of up to 15,000 Nepali citizens recruited for Russia’s war, with Nepal’s foreign minister confirming at least 14 deaths and formally asking Russia to return hundreds of citizens.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sri Lanka’s government has acknowledged around 280 citizens recruited to fight on both sides of the war, while UN Special Rapporteurs formally raised allegations with Moscow in July 2025 documenting Sri Lankans trafficked and forcibly conscripted through false job offers.
India’s Central Bureau of Investigation identified at least 35 citizens duped into travelling to Russia through recruitment agents, and the government has put the total figure recruited at 91 in a formal parliamentary statement. High-level diplomatic engagement has since secured Russian commitments to stop recruiting Indian nationals.
An Associated Press (AP) investigation published in early 2026 found Bangladeshi men lured with promises of civilian work and then coerced, under threat of violence or imprisonment, into front-line logistics and casualty-recovery tasks. Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters has said Russia formally agreed to stop recruiting from Sri Lanka, Nepal, India, and Pakistan after those four countries alone had sent at least 1,794 fighters combined.
Latin America, the former USSR, and now Indonesia
Cuba’s foreign ministry says it launched a crackdown on trafficking networks after discovering in 2023 that its citizens were fighting in Ukraine. Citizens of Cuba, Colombia, and Brazil have since turned up in testimony gathered by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and Amnesty alike.
Ukraine Pushes Forward in 4 Frontline Sectors as Russia Struggles for Gains
Two Chinese nationals were captured fighting for Russia in the Donetsk Oblast in April. And the pipeline keeps finding new markets. In August 2026, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service said that it had documented at least eight Indonesian citizens recruited through the same false-job, fast-passport model already tested for years on Nepal, Cuba, Kenya, and India – describing the approach as a scheme already validated on “dozens of other countries” now simply redeployed on a new one.
Even Russia’s own neighbors are treated as a recruiting pool rather than an ally’s citizenry.
Independent media tallies of intercepted recruitment data have logged 86 recruits from Tajikistan, 71 each from Uzbekistan and Belarus, 64 from Kyrgyzstan, 59 from Kazakhstan, 19 from Turkmenistan, and 12 from Moldova. Citizens of formally friendly or allied post-Soviet states, pitched with the same “become a new Russian” citizenship offer used everywhere else.
Why Russia needs all of them
The reason for this global hunt for recruits is not a mystery: Russia’s own losses in Ukraine are staggering, and it is running out of Russians willing to replace them.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff, cumulative Russian personnel losses (killed and wounded) since Feb. 24, 2022 have reached approximately 1,519,650 as of Sept. 21, 2026 – daily losses through September running consistently above 1,300 and briefly spiking past 1,900 in a single day.
Independent Western estimates are more conservative but still place Russian casualties in the region of 1.2 million, part of combined battlefield losses on both sides that analysts now put close to two million people.
This is precisely why foreign recruits are so valuable to Moscow and so disposable in its eyes. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described their fate bluntly: “Most of them are immediately sent to the so-called ‘meat assaults,’ where they are quickly killed. Most mercenaries do not survive more than a month.”
Untrained, unable to communicate in Russian, and with no support network on the ground, foreign recruits are disproportionately used to open assaults ahead of trained units – absorbing the first, heaviest casualties, so that experienced Russian soldiers do not have to.
What happens when they don’t come home
A WhatsApp correspondence obtained for this story, with a contact representing several Ugandan families of recruits killed or missing in Russia’s war, shows exactly what these families face once the fighting is over for their relative – whether he survived it or not. The identity of the contact is withheld for their protection. The number that opened the exchange is a Uganda-registered line. The exchange opened with the question at the center of every one of these cases:
Contact: “Some families went to Russia for the repatriation of remains and compensation but unfortunately they got nothing. How can the families get help in this case?”
The reply did not soften the reality:
Ukrainian side: “This comes as no surprise – this is Russia, after all. They have no interest in returning foreign prisoners of war, or in paying them compensation, or providing assistance to their families in the event of their death. No such cases have yet been recorded. At present, the only way forward is to publicize these stories in the media so that they gain public attention. Perhaps then, the Russian Federation will take some action to meet the needs of these families. Alongside this, it is necessary to take the matter to an international court, but this requires evidence that their relative signed a contract providing for payments in the event of death, and so on. But Russia will deny everything, it will be difficult to prove. In any case, publicity is needed.”
The Ukrainian side then asked the only question that matters in court or in print:
Ukrainian side: “Tell me, do these families have any documents from the Russian government? Any replies or refusals regarding the payment of funds? You do realize that mere words are just words. To substantiate claims in the media or in court, evidence is required.”
The contact then described documentation that, unusually, had already reached government level:
Contact: “We have a few examples of contracts, visas, and letters from the Ministry of Defense Department of Sub Saharan Africa.”
Contact: “Family traveled to Russia but no remains available nor compensation.”
Asked to clarify whether those letters had come from African defense ministries writing to Moscow, the contact corrected the address:
Contact: “This is a department in Russia defense that handles African cases, unfortunately when families get to Russia they are denied access to a facility. I don’t know how this issue can be addressed.”
Ukrainian side: “Do you mean the Russian Federation’s African Corps?”
Contact: “I will share a copy, it’s confidential.”
The files that followed were not Africa Corps letterhead. They were the embassy covering letters and the Russian foreign ministry notes on Benon, Mutesigensi, and Mwesigwa.
The reply confirmed the scale of the wider machine rather than answering the Africa Corps question directly:
Ukrainian side: “On the Russian side, the participation of foreign nationals from more than 130 different countries has already been confirmed. They lure these people to Russia under false pretenses, where they are forced or tricked into signing contracts with the Russian Armed Forces. And then, after a week of training, they are sent straight into hell.”
The contact raised a second, less-documented layer of harm – families already grieving being targeted a second time by people posing as fixers:
Contact: “How can we get help? From what I see I think there are cartels trying to swindle compensations and there is also a big challenge with accountability. Majority of our people are missing on all lists, we tried to check on Ukrainian chat bot ‘I want to find.’”
Ukrainian side: “To make sure your people aren’t deceived by scammers or others, just remember that Russia does not pay any compensation to foreign citizens.”
Ukrainian side: “Yes, this is the bot for the Coordination Headquarters on the Treatment of Prisoners of War.”
When pressed further, the Ukrainian side was explicit about what it can and cannot do. It can gather information on missing foreigners, but cannot extract payment or accountability from Moscow:
Ukrainian side: “We do not disseminate or publicize any sensitive information, but we do collect, study, and analyze it. We strive to help families searching for their relatives – there are tens of thousands of them around the world – given Russia’s extensive influence and capabilities. We are working to counter the recruitment of foreign citizens into the ranks of the Russian Armed Forces. This will benefit both your people and ours.”
The contact’s response captured the grievance driving families toward any channel willing to listen:
Contact: “They don’t have information about our people, and Russia doesn’t give any accountability at all, it’s been eight months of no communication.”
Ukrainian side: “Yes, because we gather this information bit by bit.”
At that point, the contact shared two scanned documents bearing the letterhead of the Embassy of the Republic of Uganda in Moscow: a three-page disappearance file on Kamusiye Benon and a two-page death notice on Alex Mutesigensi and Baker Mwesigwa. They were formal diplomatic instruments, not informal testimony, showing that Kampala’s own mission has already engaged Moscow on paper over specific citizens. The contact then described the practical burden families carry even before they learn about an outcome:
Contact: “Make research please, the poor families struggle to raise money for tickets, visas, document legalization, hotels, but when they get to Russia, they aren’t getting addressed.”
The final substantive reply is, in effect, the bluntest available summary of where every one of these families currently stands, regardless of nationality:
Ukrainian side: “We will look for information about your citizens, but that is all we can do. We understand you and your efforts to uncover the truth, but I must emphasize once again that this is how the Russians treat everyone. Therefore, I cannot help you obtain compensation, since Russia is a terrorist state, and you will receive nothing from them. However, we can draw public attention to this issue, and then the international community will put pressure on Russia and perhaps force them to pay all reparations, as well as compensation to the families of those who died because of their actions.”
The contact’s closing message pointed to the one avenue Uganda itself has offered so far, and its evident limits:
Contact: “Our ambassador says compensation is possible but we don’t have a clear process. I think families should be allowed to interface with the responsible Russian ministries handling compensation.”
That is the trap inside the notes themselves. Russia writes that payments are “provided for.” The ambassador forwards the invitation to come and collect. The families sell assets for tickets and certified translations. Then, they say, the door stays closed: no remains, no money, and a second market of fixers offering to “process” a compensation that does not arrive.
Main takeaway
Every recruitment pitch described above – from Kampala to Kathmandu, Jakarta to Dushanbe – sells the same three things: fast money, a fast passport, and a job nowhere near a battlefield.
Every documented outcome delivers the same three things instead: a Russian-language contract no one explains, a front-line assignment inside weeks, and – for hundreds already confirmed dead and thousands more unaccounted for – silence.
Russia’s own notes to Uganda speak of payments “provided for by legislative and other regulatory legal acts.” No country’s ministry of defense has produced a single confirmed case of those payments reaching a foreign recruit’s family. No embassy correspondence reviewed for this story, or in the wider reporting cited here, describes Russia returning a body without months or years of pressure, if at all.
The gap between the loud promise and what a person actually ends up receiving is not an accident here. It is an iron pattern, repeating itself in every documented case.
But there is a deeper dimension to this cynical calculation. Russia’s Ministry of Defense has kept official casualty figures under wraps since September 2022, and the one number the Kremlin ever gave at the start of the full-scale invasion, independent researchers openly describe as a several-fold undercount. Instead, a joint project by the BBC’s Russian Service and Mediazona painstakingly rebuilds the list of Russian dead from obituaries, state death payments to families, and fresh cemetery records.
As of Sept. 21, 2026, they had confirmed the names of at least 258,989 dead Russian service members, not an official government tally, but names gathered from obituaries, payouts, and grave records. Foreigners among them number 1,285, plus 2,304 fighters from North Korea, for a combined total of 3,589 as of July 2026.
The investigators themselves caution that this is only the beginning: foreign recruits are far less likely to leave behind the kind of trace – a local obituary, a regional-government payment, a relative’s social media post – that the entire counting method depends on.
In the end, for Russia’s war machine, a foreign recruit is not simply someone who will later, quietly, not get paid. He is a convenient, expendable resource whose loss is almost impossible for anyone to count.

articles.title: NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
articles.body:
NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
European NATO nations should take greater responsibility for security in the Middle East, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said. He also defended the US-Israeli war on Iran and argued that European members should spend less on social programs and more on the military.
Rutte made the remarks at a Chicago Council on Global Affairs event in Iowa on Tuesday after being asked to “make the case” for NATO to Americans by explaining “what’s in it” for them.
He described the Middle East as “Europe’s backyard” and “not the United States’ backyard,” arguing that Washington’s war against Tehran was “necessary” but that the US had to launch it because “somehow the Europeans did not have enough capabilities to do it themselves.”
“In the future, what you get from a stronger NATO is that Europeans can take care of their own backyard,” Rutte said.
The US-Israeli war on Iran, launched in late February, caused major friction within NATO as several European members resisted supporting Washington’s belligerence. Spain refused to allow American warplanes to use its bases for the campaign, drawing US President Donald Trump’s ire. Germany and the UK described the conflict as “not our war,” while stopping short of condemning the US and Israel.
Trump has since repeatedly accused European allies of failing to meet their NATO commitments and claimed the bloc “was not there when we needed them.” In April, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth said NATO’s future was uncertain and Washington could not currently reaffirm its commitment to collective defense.
Rutte also argued on Tuesday that the burden within NATO was unfair because European members spend heavily “on pensions and welfare,” while Washington has to devote more resources to weapons but “would also like to spend more on all these other lofty, beautiful items, but they can’t because they have to spend so much on defense.”
He described raising NATO’s defense spending target from 2% to 5% of GDP as “the fairness element” and part of an “equalizing” process. The remarks come as Washington pushes for a reorganization dubbed NATO 3.0, under which European members would sharply increase military spending and production while assuming “primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Rutte also offered to help “protect the United States from threats of Russia” and China and prevent the Arctic “from becoming militarized by the Russians and the Chinese.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last month that Moscow was primarily interested in “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation” and accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization.” His comments followed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal earlier this year to use increased EU military spending on “Arctic-ready equipment.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called Russian leader Vladimir Putin "patient zero" who is spreading the idea of war around the world.
Source: Zelenskyy's address to the UN General Assembly in New York, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that Putin "is always looking for someone who can help him kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and attack another country" rather than stopping and running his own country.
"After all of this, can you even imagine him without war? He is 'patient zero' – the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks and, of course, new crises," the president emphasised.
Zelenskyy said that the more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.
He explained that Ukraine is targeting Russia's oil industry in an effort to stop Moscow and undermine its ability to finance the war.
"Oil itself is not Ukraine's target. It is not our target. Not gasoline or diesel, not factories or ports as such. Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive. Russia's finances and Russia's production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped," he stressed.
In this context, Zelenskyy pointed out that when anyone lifts or eases sanctions against Russia, they "give this war more time".
"And when someone in the world weakens sanctions, weakens sanctions against Russian oligarchs, it may make life more comfortable for rich Russians, but it also gives the war more time – more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone," he added.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia threatens lives in Ukraine every hour by attacking the country with drones and missiles.
"Would your country survive if, God forbid, you had to face something like this? Ukraine has," the president asked those present, urging them to join efforts to strengthen Ukraine's air defence.
Background:
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stressed during a UN Security Council meeting that Russia's war against Ukraine poses a threat to the entire world.
- It was also reported that 50 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement in support of Ukraine at the UN, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
- The previous day, US President Donald Trump called on Putin to "settle the war" against Ukraine.

The drones were launched from areas including Oryol, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia; temporarily occupied Donetsk; as well as Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea and the waters of the Sea of Azov.
The Odesa and Kyiv regions were the main targets of the attack.
The air assault was repelled by Ukrainian combat aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned-systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Thursday, September 24, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 227 targets:
- four Zircon missiles;
- three Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles;
- one Banderol/Dan-T munition;
- 219 drones.
Hits were recorded at 13 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at another 10 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with dozens of enemy UAVs still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, during the night of September 24, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones.
A 57-year-old woman was killed in the Podilskyi district and a 65-year-old man was killed in the Solomianskyi district.

articles.title: Kremlin slams EU over transfer of Russian profits to Ukraine
articles.body:
Kremlin slams EU over transfer of Russian profits to Ukraine
The EU is committing “theft” by handing over profits from frozen Russian assets to Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Some $300 billion in Moscow’s funds were blocked by the US and EU after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Around $240 billion of the sum is still being held at the Belgium-based clearing house Euroclear.
On Wednesday, high-ranking Russian Foreign Ministry official Vladislav Maslennikov told RIA Novosti that Brussels has already transferred €8 billion ($9.1 billion) in income generated by the frozen Russian assets to the government in Kiev. Some €3.5 billion from the sum has been used to purchase arms for Ukrainian forces that are fighting the Russian military, he added.
When asked to comment on the development by journalists on Thursday, Peskov replied by saying that Moscow considers such actions as illegal.
“We truly believe this is theft. And we treat it accordingly, nothing has changed in our position here,” the spokesman noted.
Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said on Tuesday that the EU is working on a new scheme to confiscate the $240 billion in Moscow’s frozen sovereign assets altogether.
The bloc’s leaders have “a vital interest in stealing Russian assets” because they fear they will not be able to indefinitely finance Ukraine on their own, it said.
EU bureaucrats in Brussels are now discussing the creation of a new supranational structure that could take control of Russian central bank funds after they are moved outside Belgium’s jurisdiction, the SVR said.
The Belgian government has repeatedly blocked proposals to seize the assets, with Prime Minister Bart De Wever warning that such a step would expose his country to legal and financial liability. Euroclear has also said it could sue the EU if the funds are confiscated.
The bloc is “in a hurry” to pull off the seizure before elections in several EU states in 2027, the SVR stated, arguing that future governments in the bloc could be less willing to back further financial support for Ukraine.
The agency also warned that the move would undermine trust in European financial institutions among major foreign investors, including China, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Singapore.
Moscow has long said that any attempt to appropriate its sovereign funds would be against the law, warning that it would trigger legal action and retaliation, potentially including measures against Western assets held in Russia.

articles.title: Former prosecutor general Kravchenko appears to have violated Vienna residency registration rules – UP
articles.body:
Former prosecutor general Kravchenko appears to have violated Vienna residency registration rules – UP
Former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko appears to have violated the rules concerning his registered place of residence after moving to Vienna.
Source: an article by Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach
Details: The address listed in a document from the Austrian register is not Kravchenko's place of residence, as required by law.
Apartment No. 12 in the building at 7 Jordangasse is not a residential property but the office of CS Corporate Services GmbH. On its website, the company offers four services: domiciliation, meaning a registered legal address for Austrian limited liability companies; secretarial services; management services; and the sale of shelf companies that are already registered and ready to be transferred to a new owner.
The description of its domiciliation service says that an address in Vienna's first district, a few minutes' walk from the central square Stephansplatz, is registered with the Commercial Court, tax authorities and municipal authorities, while staff receive clients' post and, on their instructions, forward it unopened, scan it or reply to it themselves.
At least two dozen other legal entities are registered at the same address. They include subsidiaries of genuine international companies such as Duracell Austria GmbH and KPLER GmbH, but most are little-known companies, including Numitor, Febania, Nobeka, Furninet, Code Panda IT Solutions and others.
Kravchenko and his wife may have taken this step to conceal their actual place of residence in Vienna.
Registration in Vienna may also indicate that Kravchenko plans to establish legal residence in the Austrian capital, as it is well known that Austria does not extradite people wanted by Ukraine.
Tkach noted that when speaking to an influential official about the fate of Ukrainian officials in Austria, he had heard a wry comment: "At this rate, Vienna will soon have an entire Ukrainian government-in-exile."
Apart from the prosecutor general, who appears to have registered in Vienna only recently, the city is already home to former constitutional court chairman Oleksandr Tupytskyi, former National Bank governor Kyrylo Shevchenko, former MP Andrii Kholodov and many other "former" officials who have largely become stranded in one of Europe's best cities for years, either because of the war or to avoid punishment.
"In a city where there are no air-raid warnings, ballistic missiles, notices of suspicion issued by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) or the need to pay bail. In a city that does not extradite people wanted by Ukraine. For now," Tkach added.
Previously: It was reported that Kravchenko had left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September, travelling abroad in a luxury taxi rather than an official vehicle and crossing the border at the Shehyni-Medyka checkpoint.
It is also known that Kravchenko submitted a letter of resignation from the prosecution service. It was accepted, and Kravchenko was dismissed from the prosecution service on 21 September.
Background:
- On 7 September, Kravchenko resigned as prosecutor general amid an investigation by NABU and SAPO into the alleged "protection" of scam call centres.
- On 14 September, Kravchenko said he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU director Semen Kryvonos and accused NABU and SAPO of seizing materials from criminal proceedings against employees of the anti-corruption agencies in the course of searches conducted as part of Operation Carthage.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in law enforcement, Kravchenko left Ukraine in an official car on the night of 13-14 September.
- He said in a statement that he had left to go on an official trip. According to an order by the prosecutor general dated 13 September, a copy of which was seen by Ukrainska Pravda, Kravchenko left for Paris for five days "to take part in PACE hearings on Ukrainian children". However, he was not listed among the speakers on the event agenda.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) to back Kravchenko's dismissal as prosecutor general.
- On 14 September, Zelenskyy signed a decree suspending Kravchenko as prosecutor general. The Verkhovna Rada later voted in favour of his dismissal.
- As of 21 September, Kravchenko, whose official trip abroad ended on 18 September, had not returned to work.

articles.title: Russians hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles: two killed, eight injured – photos
articles.body:
Russians hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles: two killed, eight injured – photos
Two people are known to have been killed and eight injured in a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the night of 23-24 September.
Source: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko; Kyiv City Military Administration; State Emergency Service of Ukraine
Quote from Klitschko: "One person has been killed and two others injured in the capital. Medics have taken both the injured people to hospital."
Details: Since the beginning of the night there had been reports of several waves of ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, numerous explosions in the capital, damage caused, and calls for medical assistance.
Klitschko also said a house in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district had been partially destroyed after debris fell in the courtyard of a private property. There may be people trapped under the rubble.
In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on a car park near a medical facility, causing vehicles to catch fire.
Update: Klitschko later reported that windows and part of the facade of a maternity hospital in the Podilskyi district had been damaged after missile debris fell nearby.
Early reports indicate that there are no casualties at the medical facility.
However, Klitschko said that one person had been killed in a car park near the facility.
A nearby medical diagnostic centre was also damaged.
"As of now, two people have been killed and three injured in the capital. All those injured have been taken to hospital," he stated.
He also reported that debris had fallen at two more locations in the Dniprovskyi district, both on the grounds of private properties. One of the houses was damaged.
Missile debris fell onto a road in the Darnytskyi district.
Quote from Klitschko at 03:00: "Two people have been killed and five injured in the capital. Three of those injured have been taken to hospital. Two are in a critical condition."

In the Podilskyi district, a fire broke out involving four cars in a car park following the strike near the maternity hospital. The fire was extinguished and a body was found.
At another location, a single-storey non-residential building caught fire. This fire was also extinguished.
In the Dniprovskyi district, another person was injured, while a fire in an office building was also extinguished.

articles.title: Pakistan launches precision airstrikes on Afghanistan following thwarted drone attack from border
articles.body:
Pakistan conducted airstrikes on 10 locations in Afghanistan that it said were being used to launch and store drones, some of which had been used against Pakistan a day earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Thursday.
The strikes come as tensions escalate between the allies-turned-foes, who have long been at odds over attacks by Islamist militants, which also triggered their worst fighting in years in February.
Islamabad accuses Kabul of harboring militants who stage cross-border attacks, but Afghanistan's Taliban government denies harboring anti-Pakistani insurgents and says militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Pakistan's air defense systems detected drones launched from Afghan territory on Wednesday, which were tracked and neutralized before they could reach any of their intended targets, Tarar said in a post on X/Twitter.
Pakistan then conducted the "precision aerial and drone strikes" on 10 locations, which were "limited to identified military objectives" linked to the attempted attacks, he said.
Afghan Taliban will be met with 'firm and resolute response'
"Any further provocative act by Afghan Taliban will be responded with firm and resolute response," the minister said.
The Pakistani airstrikes were conducted in several areas of the southeastern Khost province, Mustaghfir Gurbaz, spokesperson for the Khost governor, said.
There were no casualties, he said. However, a Taliban spokesperson said that four were killed in the strikes.
An attack on a police facility in northwestern Pakistan last week, which killed at least 24 people, has reignited fighting between the countries after nearly three months of relative calm.
Pakistan's government earlier this week also said it had launched airstrikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants, while Afghan Taliban officials accused Islamabad of killing three civilians in overnight strikes on Afghan territory.
The worst single incident, however, occurred in March, when more than 400 people were killed in a Pakistani airstrike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation center.
Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure."

articles.title: Russia launched massive attack on Odesa region - Romania scrambled F-16s and F-18s, while Moldova closed part of its airspace because of drones
articles.body:
Russia launched massive attack on Odesa region - Romania scrambled F-16s and F-18s, while Moldova closed part of its airspace because of drones
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked civilian targets in Odesa region, injuring two people. Because of the drones, Romania scrambled fighter jets, while Moldova closed part of its airspace.
Russia launched a massive attack on the Odesa region during the night of September 24. Against this backdrop, Romania scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and two Spanish F-18s, while Moldova closed its airspace in the north of the country because of drones flying overhead. UNN reports this, citing data from Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper and the defense ministries of both neighboring countries.
What are the consequences in the Odesa region
This night, Russia carried out a massive combined attack on civilian infrastructure in the Odesa region. A hospital, a gymnasium, residential buildings, a shopping center, warehouses, and other civilian facilities came under attack. Two people were injured
According to him, as a result of the attack:
-  a 10-story non-residential building was damaged; 
-  the shopping center that had previously been attacked was damaged; 
-  the roof of a municipal hospital department and food warehouses were damaged; 
-  the windows of the gymnasium and residential buildings were shattered, and cars were damaged. 
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine showed the consequences of Russia's massive attack on the Odesa region.
Romania scrambled fighter jets
"On the morning of Thursday, September 24, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defense detected an aerial target moving over Ukrainian territory near the border with Romania, in the northern part of Botoșani County," Romania's Ministry of Defense said in a statement.
Two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft, which are on combat air-policing duty, took off from the 86th Air Base in Borcea to monitor the situation. According to radar signals, the aerial target entered national airspace through the northern part of Botoșani County
Measures were taken to alert the population in Botoșani and Suceava counties, and at 06:26 an RO-Alert message was issued.
The aerial target remained in national airspace for approximately four minutes, after which it crashed near the town of Solca, Suceava County, without casualties or material damage. Response teams from the Ministry of Internal Affairs arrived at the scene, secured the perimeter, and identified a small unmanned aerial vehicle; there was no fire at the crash site
At 07:21, an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter took off from the 95th Air Base in Bacău, Romania, to monitor the situation in the area, according to the statement.
"Also, during the night of September 23-24, a group of aerial targets was detected north of the village of Kiliya-Veke, on the territory of Ukraine, near the border with Romania," the statement said.
Two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Force, which are part of the enhanced air-policing combat duty, took off from the Mihail Kogălniceanu 57th Air Base to monitor the situation
At 04:41, an RO-Alert message was issued for residents of the northern part of Tulcea County. The air raid alert for the northern part of Tulcea County ended at 05:44.
Moldova closed part of its airspace
Moldova's defense authorities reported, "in the context of the Russian Federation's massive attacks on Ukraine," the "detection of an unauthorized flight through the national airspace by an unmanned aerial vehicle, which entered the airspace of the Republic of Moldova at 06:14 (...) and crossed the state border." "At 06:16, the aerial object left the national airspace," the statement said.
In addition, "today, at 5:21, a patrol of the border police of the Republic of Moldova observed another unidentified object. (...) It later left the national airspace."
Later, Moldova's defense authorities also stated that "another object crossed the national airspace at 6:35, (...) and at 6:45 it was observed by citizens."
The country's Air Operations Service also reported "another drone that flew through the airspace at 06:58. (...) At 07:11, the object disappeared from monitoring systems in the vicinity of the village of Cunicea."
"For security reasons, the airspace of the Republic of Moldova in the northern part has been closed," the statement said.
"At 7:46, the airspace in the north was reopened," the country's defense authorities said.

In a keynote speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Lee laid out a long-term, step-by-step sequence for pursuing the ultimate goal of North Korea’s denuclearisation. articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
Ukrainian president urges world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues to impede its war efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has singled out Russian President Vladimir Putin as the reason for the continuing war between the two neighbouring countries, urging world leaders to sustain economic pressure on Moscow during his address at the United Nations General Assembly.
“For nearly five years now, Russia’s generals have tried to carry out Putin’s crazy war,” Zelenskyy said, adding that no one openly supported this war “except for one man”.
Zelenskyy said Russia had lost 248,000 soldiers over the last eight months in Ukraine, managing to capture “a little more than 1,000 square kilometres [386 square miles] of our territory this year”.
“Putin spent 248 people for every kilometre. Does anyone still think he is smart?” he said, adding that the numbers “are not just statistics. This is about people”.
“We have archived footage of thousands and thousands of Russians losing their lives in kill zones. This is what Putin wants,” he said.
“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, ‘That’s it. Enough. Peace,'” Zelenskyy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘patient zero’, the one from whom war keeps spreading further. ‘Patient zero’ must be stopped,” he said.
Zelenskyy said he expects Russia to intensify its bombing campaign on the country in the coming months and that Ukrainians are prepared for a harsh winter.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it harsh for Russia too,” he said.
This month, Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border. Another attack on Sunday forced a Moscow oil refinery to halt crude processing.
Russia also slammed jet-powered drones into two petrol stations and other sites in Kyiv, killing one and injuring at least seven people on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has been pushing for an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, blaming the war between the two as one reason behind skyrocketing fuel prices.
Zelenskyy called for sustained economic pressure, saying the money Russia earned through trade “gives this war more time”.
“And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.
Last week, Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia over its war in Ukraine, days after US Congress sent the bill to the White House with rare bipartisan support.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy also claimed that nationals of 47 countries are fighting alongside Russia in Ukraine, mentioning the two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region last year, who were sent to South Korea by Kyiv.
“Why should Koreans give their lives in a war in Ukraine?” he asked.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Moscow is prepared to negotiate towards a lasting peace with Ukraine, but won’t just “pause” the war, arguing that such a pause would buy Ukraine and its backers time to line up more weapons.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says both Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments and each country’s energy sectors.

articles.title: Trump fetes China's Xi with lavish White House welcome
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Donald Trump fetes China's Xi with lavish White House welcome
US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday for a day full of pageantry with one goal—keeping the fragile peace between the rival superpowers.
Trump personally greeted Xi on the tarmac after his arrival on Wednesday, the first time in more than six decades that a US president has welcomed a foreign political leader at Joint Base Andrews near Washington.
He will lay on more pomp and ceremony for Xi on Thursday, treating him to a formal welcome on the White House South Lawn, a military flyover, talks in the Oval Office and finally a grand state banquet.
But the lavish welcome masks deep tensions over thorny topics including the trade war between the world's top two economies, artificial intelligence and Beijing's diplomatic and economic support for Iran.
Xi urged cooperation in comments reported by Chinese state media shortly after his arrival, saying that China and the United States should be "partners rather than rivals."
The Chinese president added that he was looking "forward to in-depth exchanges with President Trump on major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation."
Trade truce
An early piece of good news for Beijing and Washington was the announcement by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Wednesday of a two-month extension of a trade truce that was due to expire in November.
Both sides are keen to avoid plunging back into the trade war sparked by the US president's sweeping global tariffs last year.
But while Trump boasts that he will get results from what he calls his "great relationship" with Xi -- the latest in a series of authoritarian leaders he has befriended -- few breakthroughs are expected.
Instead their third meeting since Trump returned to power is aimed at maintaining the broader detente despite the underlying tensions.
Xi's first White House state visit in more than a decade will therefore be more about spectacle than substance.
The program includes a military inspection in the Rose Garden—which Trump recently paved over—and a gift giving ceremony involving Trump's wife Melania and Xi's wife Peng Liyuan.
Trump and Xi will make remarks in the morning and again in the evening, though it remains unclear if there will be an opportunity for reporters to put questions to the two leaders.
The state dinner will feature a host of top US tech and AI company bosses—although Xi's delegation includes no CEOs, sources told AFP.
'Great greeting'
Trump set the tone on Wednesday when he and Melania met the Chinese presidential couple on a red carpet at Joint Base Andrews, before a military band played the national anthems and US bombers flew noisily overhead.
"I thought it was a great little meeting, a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it," Trump told reporters—brushing off the fact that Xi had not welcomed him at the airport for his Beijing state visit in May.
Trump confirmed that his stalled Iran war would be on the agenda, despite earlier playing down reports that Beijing was giving Tehran intelligence.
"I'll be talking about that and many other subjects—but it's all coming along well, including that," Trump said.
Artificial intelligence is also set to dominate the summit amid growing fears that it risks wiping out humanity—even as China and the United States race for supremacy in the field.
Taiwan will also be on the cards, with Trump's words likely to be watched for any sign of diminishing US support for the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.
Xi's visit will wrap up on Friday morning when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.

articles.title: Canada and UK could merge war chests to fight Russia – media
articles.body:
Canada and UK could merge war chests to fight Russia – media
Canada and the UK are considering merging two major military financing initiatives to help European NATO members and other Kiev backers finance their military buildup against Russia, the CBC reported on Wednesday, citing anonymous officials.
In recent years, European NATO nations have increasingly accused Moscow of preparing an attack on members of the US-led military bloc, using the alleged threat to justify bloated military budgets. Moscow has denied any such intention.
Canada is leading plans for the Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), while the UK is pushing for the Multilateral Defense Mechanism (MDM). Both initiatives are intended to make it easier for allied states to finance military purchases and expand arms production.
In July, Carney failed to entice then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer to join the DSRB as a founding member. However, Burnham’s government is more aligned with Canada on the issue, the CBC reported, citing an anonymous Canadian official.
Ottawa is confident the two countries will reach a deal to combine their initiatives into a joint institution, the Canadian Press reported last week, citing a senior Canadian official.
So far, Ottawa’s DSRB has attracted support from Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Türkiye, and Ukraine. The Netherlands, Finland, and Poland have backed the UK’s MDM.
The plans come as NATO countries escalate their military spending. Last year, following pressure from US President Donald Trump, bloc members agreed to invest 5% of their GDP annually in their militaries and defense-related areas by 2035.
In the meantime, European NATO members have increasingly touted the Russian threat to militarize and prepare the continent for a potential war with Moscow, all while insulating the US from the consequences of such a conflict.
“European elites… now seek to frighten their populations with a mythical Russian threat,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalists at a BRICS summit earlier in September, stressing that Moscow has “no grounds for any conflict with Europe.”

articles.title: Trump gives Chinese leader a warm welcome; will discuss trade, Taiwan and AI
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump gave Chinese President Xi Jinping a warm welcome—greeting him with a military flypast and a 30-meter-long red carpet—to kick off the Chinese leader’s three-day visit to Washington, the BBC reports.
In an unusual move, Trump and the First Lady greeted Xi’s delegation at the airport. Xi’s first visit to Washington since 2015 is expected to include closed-door meetings, an official dinner, and discussions on a range of issues—from artificial intelligence to the war in Iran and the situation regarding Taiwan—as well as talks on extending the trade truce.
Following the welcome at the Maryland airport, where the leaders and their wives exchanged pleasantries, Trump and his guests traveled to Washington in separate vehicles. This marks the first time since 1962 that a US president has personally greeted a foreign leader at an air force base, underscoring the great importance Trump attaches to Xi’s visit. In 1962, then-US President John F. Kennedy personally welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan. On the 23rd of September, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the United States and China would extend their trade truce until January. The agreement—under which Trump lowered import tariffs on certain categories of goods in exchange for the easing of restrictions on Chinese rare-earth minerals—was set to expire on the 10th of November. Bessent announced the change following a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, noting that the two had discussed the possibility of concluding a more substantial trade deal between the nations.
In a statement published by the Chinese state media outlet Xinhua, Xi remarked that
both China and the United States are great nations and their people are great people.
He emphasized that the two countries should be partners rather than rivals.
US First Lady Melania Trump told Fox News that she had been closely involved in planning the visit’s agenda and that Trump had decided to personally welcome Xi at the airport, given their good relationship.
Xi is accompanied on the visit by Cai Qi, a member of the Chinese Communist Party Politburo Standing Committee; Vice Premier He Lifeng; Foreign Minister Wang Yi; and other delegates and envoys from Beijing. In an official statement, Xi indicated that the rejuvenation of the Chinese people and the strengthening of America can coexist, reinforce one another, and benefit the world. He added that he is confident the visit will yield fruitful results.
It is not known whether representatives from the business community are accompanying Xi. The entry of Chinese companies into the US market could raise new questions regarding Chinese business practices, state subsidies, and industrial overcapacity—issues that might attract more scrutiny than Xi or his party would desire. Trump was accompanied on his visit to Beijing in May by representatives from a number of major US technology companies, including Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. Executives from US artificial intelligence companies are also expected to attend the lavish official dinner on the 24th of September. Xi’s visit will conclude on the 25th of September.
Trump has previously dismissed warnings about the potential threats posed by artificial intelligence
as a fabrication, while China and the US are engaged in a race for leadership in the field.
The US president will seek to reach agreements regarding trade and import tariffs. So far, China has refrained from promising to purchase more American agricultural products or sell more rare-earth minerals. David Firestein, a representative of the Bush China Foundation, said he expects Xi to try to persuade Trump to delay or even halt the 14 billion dollars arms sale to Taiwan approved by Congress. He noted that these are long-standing points of contention between the US and China, though relations are currently more stable than they were a year ago.
Xi’s visit comes at a time when American attitudes toward China appear to be warming. A recent poll indicates that 41% of Americans view China’s territorial ambitions as a threat to the US; in 2022, that figure stood at 52%. More than half—57%—of Americans believe the US should cooperate with Beijing.
